speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of Slate for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT OF CANADIAN AMBASSADOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members may recall that on January 28 last, when I announced the opening of a new diplomatic mission in Nigeria, the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) asked me whether I could inform the house of the government's intention about the appointment of an ambassador to Mexico.
I now wish to inform the house that the government of Mexico has given its agreement to the appointment of Mr. William Arthur Irwin as Canadian ambassador to that country.
Mr. Irwin distinguished himself as assistant editor, managing editor and then editor of Maclean's magazine from 1925 to 1950. At that time he entered the public service of Canada as commissioner and chairman of the national film board, a post which he held until his appointment as Canadian high commissioner to Australia in 1953. In January, 1957 he was transferred from Australia to Brazil as ambassador, where he served until his return to Canada last September. Last fall Mr. Irwin became a member of the Canadian delegation to the fourteenth session of the United Nations general assembly in New York, where his knowledge of Latin-American affairs and his ability to establish contacts with Latin-American delegations was most helpful.
Mr. Irwin has thus had useful and varied experience in and outside the public service and as a diplomat. As ambassador to Brazil particularly he had an excellent opportunity to observe at close range the economic, political and social problems of Latin-America. I am sure that Mr. Irwin will use his diplomatic experience and his knowledge of Latin-America to help fulfil the common desire of the Mexican and Canadian governments to strengthen their already close and friendly relations, as evidenced by the highly successful visit of His Excellency President Adolfo Lopez Mateos of Mexico to Ottawa last October, and soon to be re-emphasized by the visit of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) to Mexico next April.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: HOGS-INQUIRY AS TO CHANGE IN PREMIUM PAYMENTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as pigs are in the news, I should like to ask the Minister of Agriculture whether it is the intention of the government to increase the premium on grade A hogs and withdraw the premium on grade B hogs, as suggested by the breed associations. And as a result of urgent requests for more space, does the government intend to build a new swine testing station or to enlarge the present one at Waterloo, Ontario?

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
maintopic: HOGS-INQUIRY AS TO CHANGE IN PREMIUM PAYMENTS
speechtext:
In answer to the first question may I say that whilst the breed associations request that the premium be paid only on grade A hogs and be increased to $3, and at the same time that the premium be removed from grade B hogs, a number of other farm organizations have made strong representations that this action should not be taken until a fair length of time has been given in the way of notice that this was going to be done. As a result, when we changed the grade regulations last October we announced that premium payments would be devoted entirely to grade A hogs at some time in the future. No decision has been made as to when this action will actually be taken.
As far as the latter question is concerned, may I say that there are no present plans to enlarge the swine testing station at Waterloo, Ontario. In explanation of that statement I think I should add that the R.O.P. policy for swine has been revised recently. Formal advanced registry on the basis of litter carcass scores at official test stations has been discontinued. With this change we have taken the position with swine breeders that a considerable amount of litter testing, to determine the performance of breeding stock, can be done at home. We think it is impractical to provide public testing facilities for all the litter testing that needs to be done for swine improvement.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: ATOMIC WEAPONS
subsubtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 should like to reply to a question which was asked by the Leader of the Opposition on Friday last. The question was:
Now that the Prime Minister no doubt has had an opportunity of considering the statement of the President of the United States on the sharing of atomic energy information, has he any comment to make on that statement, with special reference to the President's remark that the United States laws should be liberalized, in his view, in respect of those friends and allies on whom they could count in time of trouble?
As a preface to my remarks, and with leave of the house, I would draw attention once again to the position of the government as stated in this house on February 20, 1959; namely, that the Canadian government believes in the importance of limiting the spread of nuclear weapons at the independent disposal of national governments and that, as a matter of policy, it does not intend to undertake the production of nuclear weapons in Canada.
As to the sharing of atomic energy information, it will be recalled that I tabled in the house on May 25 of last year an agreement for co-operation with the United States on the uses of atomic energy for mutual defence purposes. This agreement was concerned principally with the conditions under which Canada can receive certain categories of restricted information and equipment required by our armed forces. By means of this agreement we are now able to obtain all the information and equipment necessary to meet our immediately foreseeable requirements.
In so far as the President's remarks at his press conference may be related to atomic 79951-0-55J
Inquiries of the Ministry weapons, I do not think it would be proper for me to elaborate on what he has said, but I should like to draw the attention of the house to a statement issued by the White House on Friday last which reads as follows:
The question of possible amendments to the atomic energy act in relation to the transfer of nuclear weapons, or information concerning them, to other friendly nations is, like all major policy matters, under continuing review within the executive branch. There is no executive proposal now before congress, nor in preparation, for amendments to the act in either of these respects.
The house will now understand why I quoted the statement in question in view of the earlier remarks of the President.
If any changes are made in United States policies they will, of course, be taken into account in discussions which we will have with the United States authorities as to these matters. I might add that if and when Canada does acquire nuclear weapons it will be in accordance with our own national policies and with our obligations under the North Atlantic treaty.

speechtext: I should like to direct to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys a question of which I gave notice this morning. speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Comiois (Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: TSABLE RIVER, VANCOUVER ISLAND    REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE IN KEEPING MINE OPEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Vancouver East for giving me notice of this question. I have received a number of representations about the Tsable river mine. The impending withdrawal of Canadian Collieries Resources Limited from the operation of this mine has been a concern of the dominion coal board and myself for a considerable time.

Inquiries of the Ministry
It does not appear likely that the company will change its decision to withdraw. However, as hon. members from British Columbia probably know, a group at Cumberland have a plan to take over the mine and operate it on a reduced scale. An application was received from this group for a loan under the Coal Production Assistance Act.
This application had to be submitted by the dominion coal board to the Department of Justice for a ruling on whether it met the terms of the act as laid down by parliament. The Department of Justice found that it did not meet those terms. The loan, therefore, could not be granted. This occurred late in October and early in November. Since then we have received no new or revised application from the Cumberland group for a loan within the terms of the act, though we have attempted to explore other possibilities of assistance.
I may say further, Mr. Speaker, that the chairman of the dominion coal board and I held a conference in Ottawa on January 25 with a senior representative of one of the interests concerned in the Tsable river matter. This gentleman has now returned to the west and I have some hopes that the ideas we discussed may be useful in the situation.

Inquiries of the Ministry

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: USE OF SYNTHETIC HORMONE TO FATTEN CATTLE AND POULTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can assure the hon. member that poultry producers in this country are no longer obtaining synthetic hormones to inject into their poultry.
As far as cattle are concerned the synthetic product, stilbestrol, is used in the fattening process, but in very small quantities and under a feeding plan that was investigated at length by my department's food and drug directorate before being approved. The directorate has maintained its interest in this matter and to date has not found any residue of stilbestrol in the slaughtered animals. As I told the hon. member in reply to a similar question a year ago, the regulations under the Food and Drugs Act specifically prohibit the sale of poultry for food purposes if it contains any residue of added hormones.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I should like to refer, while discussing this estimate, to a number of incidents which arose out of the debate which took place the other day, and in particular to the headlines that are appearing in western newspapers over an article carried by the Canadian Press which, I think completely misrepresents what happens in this house. One story carried in the Winnipeg Free Press on

February 6 bore the headline "Are Prairie Farmers Pampered? Comments in the House Indicate Some M.P.'s Think So."
I think if those who wrote the headline were to read the whole article this type of headline would not appear. The one in the Winnipeg Free Press is very similar to the one appearing in the Winnipeg Tribune and in another of the prairie newspapers.
I believe the remarks made in the house the other day by all hon. members who spoke, whether from the fishing communities of the east coast or the fruit growing areas of the west, made it clear that there was no one in this house who opposed the payment being made under the supplementary estimate to the western farmers. I think, in the main, that not only did hon. members approve these payments but that in many cases they felt the amount should be increased, not eliminated. I believe consideration should be given by some of the newspapers to the actual news which is contained in the stories rather than turning out headlines of this nature which are completely erroneous.
Nevertheless I think this draws attention to a question which this government should consider, namely a policy which would apply equally to all segments of agriculture which met with disaster or suffered unduly from the type of problem which affects farmers in western Canada. If it is proper that assistance should be given to the western farmers-and this has certainly been indicated by every hon. member who has spoken on this estimate-then there should be a policy which would make it possible for fruit growers in British Columbia to get a similar type of assistance. It should be possible for the grain farmers of Ontario to get this type of assistance, and the same measures for relief should apply to all the other segments of agriculture. I think it is time this government developed an over-all policy which would apply in times of disaster or special need to all farmers, no matter what products they happen to raise.
In the course of the considerable discussion which took place with regard to this particular estimate a question was raised by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate which I think deserves much more consideration than it has been given by the government. I refer to the manner in which this type of legislation has been introduced. It would appear that the government has been willing to accept the criticism of the Liberals in opposition and to reply to it by saying, "We are not doing anything you did not do. By introducing this payment in a supplementary estimate we are following the precedent

which you yourselves set up when you were on the government benches". I do not think this is an answer to the criticism that this matter should have been introduced by a resolution, giving members an opportunity to link this particular measure with the over-all assistance given to farmers and the overall agricultural program. This procedure would enable hon. members to reach a much better understanding of how this assistance will fit in with the government's general program.
I feel the farmers of the west can rest assured that every member of this house is interested in helping farmers who have suffered because of unreasonable weather conditions in western Canada. 1 think they have the right to know that, and certainly the government was not wrong in telling them so. I think also that the provincial governments which have been asked to give assistance to their people should be assured of cooperation from the federal government.
The Prime Minister says no such assurances were given. I think such assurances should have been given. I believe a province which has been asked to make a large contribution, and which would have to provide the total sum required if the federal government did not come in, should have an assurance from the federal government that some assistance will be available. I think the government has no obligation then to introduce an immediate resolution so the question can be discussed as part of an over-all program.
As the representative of a farming community in Ontario I am very pleased to support this resolution. Because of the fact that I have been in western Canada since the snowfall took place-I was out there in the fall, and know what problems these farmers face-I suggest that the amount of money now envisaged is not sufficient. I think the provincial governments are going to be asked for further assistance and will have to provide more assistance than is contemplated in this particular estimate. I believe the federal government itself will have to be more generous to these farmers than it has been. If conditions in the spring are unsatisfactory, many of these farmers will not reap any crop at all. What the precise situation will be in the spring is hypothetical, but if certain conditions are not met many of these farmers will have no prospect of a harvest. If there is an unusually wet spring there will be no return to the farmers, and this contribution will appear to be very small.
The type of headline referred to, making reference to the pampering of prairie farmers, does not reflect the opinion of hon. mem-79951-0-56

bers of this committee, nor is it a fair comment on the debate that took place in this chamber.
It has been suggested that fishermen, fruit growers and other segments of agriculture need assistance in similar circumstances. No one is suggesting that the farmers are not entitled to assistance under this system, but most are of the opinion that the amount is too small and that more money should be put into P.F.A.A. as a method of assisting those who have suffered this loss.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to support this emergency legislation to assist the farmers of western Canada I am pleased to say I am particularly interested in it because I come from a constituency in which there are 25,000 people either engaged in farming or dependent on the farming industry.
I am especially happy that the cost of the assistance provided in this way will be shared equally by the provinces and the federal government, and will apply to farmers who have more than 50 per cent of their crops under the snow up to a maximum of 200 acres.
I was keenly interested in listening to the remarks of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate on Friday last as he voiced his criticism of the method by which this emergency assistance was brought in through a supplementary estimate. I reached the conclusion that the hon. member in question is against this type of assistance. I may point out that we have a precedent for this. This is not something new in western Canada. Minister of Agriculture and the Prime Minister in this committee. My friend the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River demanded this legislation a month ago, and we could not get it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I do not think the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has a question of privilege there. As I have already indicated, if any hon. member wishes to correct any statement made by another hon. member he may do so after the hon. member who has the floor has completed his remarks. A question of privilege or point of order does not arise as the result of a difference in interpretation of the oponion or attitude of any hon. member.
Hon. gentlemen have been in the habit of raising questions of privilege and points of order which are not valid. Therefore I submit that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate will have occasion when the hon. member for Bow River has resumed his seat to make any correction he wishes to make.

Mr. Chairman, on the point of order Your Honour has raised, I was not seeking to make any correction of the hon. gentleman's statement. The hon. member made a false statement about me, and that is a question of privilege if anything is to be considered a question of privilege. In rising I demanded, in essence, that the hon. member put up or shut up.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Again I say that is not a question of privilege. If a statement does not reflect on an hon. member's character it does not give rise to a question of privilege. If it is only a question of interpreting the opinion of an hon. member it is not a question of privilege, in my mind. I do not think the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate should have insisted, because I think his last words were rather near raising a question of privilege.
Mr. Chairman, are you making the ruling that a false statement made in this committee by one hon. member about another in the course of a debate is not a question of privilege?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If I may explain further for the benefit of the Leader of the Opposition, what I said is that if a statement about an hon. member does not reflect on the character or honesty of another hon. gentleman it is not a question of privilege. If it is merely the interpretation of an attitude or an opinion of an hon. member it is not a question of privilege, and an hon. member may make any correction he desires after the hon. member who has the floor has completed his remarks. Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to put up or shut up. What I was saying was that we can be sure of this; that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was against the method we used in providing this emergency assistance, if he was not against the substance.
As I was saying before being interrupted, there are lots of precedents for what the government did. That is why I said it would appear that the hon. member may be opposed to the assistance provided by these supplementary estimates.

1 rise on another question of privilege, Mr. Chairman. The hon. gentleman is now surmising what may be in my mind, contrary to what I said in this chamber, and that is certainly a question of privilege. For the hon. member to insinuate that my statement repeatedly made in this chamber is untrue is certainly a reflection which should be withdrawn.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Anyone who suggests there is anything in your mind is obviously wrong.

Oh, a very clever
observation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. What I said earlier applies again in this case. In my opinion this is not a question of privilege. I would ask the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate to take all the notes he desires in order to reply or object to any statement made by the hon. member for Bow River after he has completed his remarks.

Mr. Chairman, if I may continue, as I was saying there are precedents for this action. In the autumn of 1951 we had circumstances in Saskatchewan and Alberta similar to those that obtained last fall. That is why I feel this type of assistance is commendable.
Now I come to another point. In this debate there has been what almost amounts to a personal attack on the Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture in reference to a certain question that was asked by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. I now have the record before me, and I think this matter should be cleared up as to what is the difference between an assurance and a contract. I propose to make the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate an offer this afternoon. I understand he is a law student. I

have a law firm in Calgary. I should like to invite the hon. gentleman to come out and article to my law firm, because my associates there would be happy to acquaint him with the difference between a contract and an assurance.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Certainly I will permit a question.
Would the hon. gentleman tell me where he got the word "contract"; because the word that was used by the Prime Minister and by me was "agreement", not "contract".

Again my hon. friend
quibbles, Mr. Chairman. The reason for my offer is now amply clear. The hon. gentleman does not know that the terms "contract" and "agreement" are synonymous, that the same definition applies to both. If my good friend will bear with me for a few minutes I will place a few things on the record to indicate what is the difference between an agreement -if that is what he wishes to call it-and an assurance. Speaking on Friday afternoon, as reported at page 796 of Hansard, the hon. member was interrupted by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and then went on to say:
The hon. member says capable, and I would also think truthful. The minister of agriculture of Manitoba said that they have a verbal agreement, but on the following Monday the Prime Minister of this country says there is no agreement. In other words, the minister of agriculture of Manitoba was lying to the legislature of Manitoba. [DOT]
Let us see what the Prime Minister said in reference to this matter when questioned by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate, as reported at page 546 of Hansard. I will put the question on record so the question and answer are together. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate asked this question:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether the government has given any other assurances to any provincial governments to share in expenditures made by those governments which have not been communicated to parliament and. if so, when the government intends to communicate such assurances to parliament?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say to the hon. gentleman that it is difficult to understand a question such as that. He has been given the answer that no agreement was entered into with any of the provinces. From the nature of the questions he continues to ask there is every indication that the hon. member-certainly speaking for himself if not for those associated with him-is in opposition to any preliminary work being done in order to meet the situation that obtains in the provinces.

Later on the Prime Minister said:
Mr. Speaker, the interest of the hon. gentleman in the field of legal semantics has been so recent, that apparently he does not understand the difference between an agreement and an assurance.
Why does the hon. member not read it all?

I say this, Mr. Chairman. Surely the hon. member by his questions is leaving a wrong impression. How can we ever come to an agreement or make a contract if we do not have some negotiations? Everyone would expect that in this type of emergency assistance the government, or the officers of the government, would meet with the provinces and discuss the problem. No doubt-I do not know; I am merely a backbencher-some assurance was given to Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta that there would be some assistance to help the farmers whose crops were under the snow. Surely when you are negotiating an agreement it is not an agreement itself, and that seems to be the point the hon. member for Bona-venture-Twillingate missed. I say this without any reservation-

It seemed to be missed
by the minister of agriculture of Manitoba, who said there was an agreement.

If the hon. member will
just bear with me for a few moments I shall explain exactly what I am driving at so far as this matter is concerned. There is a difference between an agreement and an assurance, and there is a difference between a consummated agreement and an assurance. One person can make an agreement in this regard, but there is one final condition precedent, and that is that the matter must be approved by parliament. I am sure it was in the minds of the Prime Minister and his ministers that they would come to parliament, as they are doing this afternoon, and ask parliament to approve the expenditure of $6 million to help the western farmers in their emergency.
The hon. member said that the Prime Minister had said one thing and the Minister of Agriculture another, but he was splitting hairs so far as the difference between an agreement and an assurance is concerned. When we misinterpret the terms and the facts in that regard it reminds me of a story. A fellow was sitting at home and a knock came on the door. The traveller said, "Look here, I am selling some woollens". The fellow who owned the apartment said, "Let me have a look at those woollens". After he looked at them he said, "I do not think I will buy them off you; you have only a few dirty yarns to offer". That seems to be the whole impression left in the debate

Supply-Agriculture
on the emergency assistance for the western farmers by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
I come back to my original point. We had a similar situation in 1951 and the Liberal government of that time did nothing for the western farmers. That is why there is not a Liberal member west of the great lakes today. I feel that this emergency assistance provided for in the estimate before us is going to be of great help to the farmer to assist him in paying his fuel and repair bills, and to take care of the other things that are of importance when you are operating a farming concern.
I also wish to say a few words to the hon. member for Assiniboia. I have always enjoyed listening to him. I wish to say to him today that I feel he made a tremendous speech. I have heard him make the same speech in this house on 15 different occasions, but he did a much better job the other afternoon than usual, because he was louder. He calls this legislation peanuts. To the hon. member for Assiniboia everything is peanuts. It reminds me of another story that was told to me when I was a boy. A clergyman once said, "If you good people will come out to church with all of your good friends I will show you something that has never been seen before". That sounds like the hon. member for Assiniboia. The church was packed, but what happened? The clergyman took a peanut and opened it up, and what he saw inside was a nut. Maybe that is what the hon. member for Assiniboia should do, look inside and see the problem. He should do a little real research into this problem and talk sense when he is speaking about the problems of the western farmers.
I have taken a little longer than I intended, Mr. Chairman. Before I sit down I wish to say that I completely support this emergency help provided by the government. I think it was commendable on the part of the Prime Minister and the ministers to meet with farm organizations of this country immediately the problem arose. In my own constituency much of the harvesting has been completed, because we live in the chinook belt. The fact that the Prime Minister of this country and his ministers were aware of the emergency and immediately met with the farm organizations showed that this government is concerned with the problems of the western farmers.

Mr. Chairman, as has
already been pointed out, this is an emergency measure. This estimate, and the emergency in that anxiety-ridden part of the prairies where early snow and unfavourable harvesting conditions struck with such devastating

effect, serves to underline the urgency with which this government, under the leadership of the Prime Minister and with the guidance of the Minister of Agriculture, brought forward a national crop insurance plan during the last session of parliament.
I think it can be said that the severity of conditions in western Canada at this time cannot be compared with conditions in other parts of Canada, even though they may be unfortunate. I refer to the conditions mentioned by the hon. member for Essex East and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, who incidentally never lifted their fingers when theirs were the fingers that could have written history. They made statement upon statement, acknowledging their utter lack of knowledge in regard to the situation in western Canada at this time.
This estimate can only cover a small part of the loss sustained in western Canada, and emphasizes the need of a sound, working crop insurance plan.
The Prime Minister is to be congratulated on his action in bringing this matter to the attention of Canadians everywhere, when he called together the representatives of farm organizations and leaders of governments on the prairies to deal with this particular problem. I believe the record of this government is commendable in that regard, and I think it can be favourably compared with the attitude of the provincial government in Saskatchewan in regard to the emergency situation in our province today.
As I indicated the other day, the leader of the government of our province left the province at the time of greatest anxiety to sun himself in the Mediterranean area. His ministers cannot help but know that the regulations they have brought forward have made it necessary for many people who are in need to do without the benefits of this legislation. I should like to quote from the New Year's message of the premier of Saskatchewan, who referred to this matter in these words:
The weather in the fall of 1959 dealt harshly with standing grain on many farms but our Saskatchewan farmer has never lacked fortitude and he will weather this storm as he has so many others in the past.
I would suggest to the hon. member for Assiniboia that it will take more than fortitude for the provincial government to fulfil its responsibility to those who suffer in this emergency. The hon. member for Assiniboia, the hon. member for Essex East and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate have indicated that this measure would meet with their wholehearted support if it were more universal. That is one way of indicating that their support is unwilling as

it now stands. They should not need to be reminded that the Liberal party always maintained that it could not bring a crop insurance plan into being because it infringed upon provincial rights. The C.C.F. government in Saskatchewan always abdicated their responsibility by saying that they were prepared to go ahead but could not do anything because the laissez-faire Liberals in power at Ottawa would not participate. It remained for a Conservative administration to bring forward legislation to meet both these circumstances.
At the time of the annual meeting of delegates of the Saskatchewan wheat pool, Hon. I. C. Nollet, minister of agriculture for that province, indicated that he would not jeopardize the social service program in Saskatchewan for any crop insurance plan. I can understand the impact of that slap in the face to the people of rural Saskatchewan, and I was not at all surprised when he indicated a few days later that the government would set up trial units, and would have done so sooner had it not been for the fact that the federal legislation was passed at a time when the provincial house had ended its work and the members had left for their respective homes.
All I say, Mr. Chairman, is measure that situation with the changes made in the regulations after they were originally announced by the C.C.F. in the province of Saskatchewan. It will be clearly apparent why the hon. member for Assiniboia has been so reluctant to deal with the particular measure now before us and which was also before us last Friday. He has dealt with almost everything else and kept very much away from the subject in which we are all interested.
Before we leave this item I think I should compliment the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate on the barricade he has been building between his party and the people on farms in all parts of Canada. I must confess that he divests himself of all modesty in that regard so far as the farmers of western Canada are concerned. He is gaining a certain reputation, but I assure him that his efforts to build a barrier between western and eastern Canadian farmers are doomed to disappointment.
Nonsense. He was bom on a farm.

Farm people are among the best informed of Canadian citizens today. They do not need anyone to do their thinking for them, and they do not relish the thought that every time the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate opens his mouth they get a dose of cod liver oil.
Supply-Agriculture
There is another aspect of this debate that deserves comment. It is the frequency with which the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has referred to those who speak from the government backbenches as freshmen, young and inexperienced and backbenchers. Indeed, sir, we recognize our limitations, but we do submit in all sincerity that even the least of us have an equal right to the floor of the House of Commons to express the views of our constituents. This unabashed and deliberate attempt on the part of the hon. member to shutter and silence the backbenchers on the government side is an indication of the kind of attitude they took to their own backbenchers when they sat on the other side of the house. I maintain in all sincerity that this does not justify such actions, which are not in conformity with the dignity of this committee or the symbols of democracy. I did not wish to mention this matter, but the arrogance that was displayed on Friday last brought to my mind a quotation from the works of Sir William Jones:
What constitutes a state? . .. Men who their duties know, but know their rights, and, knowing, dare maintain.

Mr. Chairman, we have had a very interesting contribution by the hon. member for Rosthern, who ranged over a very wide field. In his remarks he went out to Saskatchewan some months ago, talked about the premier having gone to Europe for a period of some three weeks, and did so in order to try to insinuate that the Saskatchewan government had abrogated its responsibility to the producers of that province. As a matter of fact the federal government was most reluctant to act, and acted only as the result of pressure exerted by three provincial governments, one of which is a Conservative government.
Even then the federal government only went half the distance in meeting the requests of the provincial governments. According to the Minister of Agriculture, in reply to a statement I made, the provincial governments presented a united front to the federal government and asked for full compensation from the federal treasury on the basis of this being a national emergency. However, the federal government made an announcement and the provinces could then either take it or leave it.
Much has been said about the Saskatchewan government's attitude to crop insurance. The Saskatchewan government can speak for itself. However, my understanding as of some weeks ago-the hon. member for Rosthern can correct me if subsequent events have made my statement inaccurate -is that farmers in Saskatchewan who

Supply-Agriculture
wish to have crop insurance will be given the chance to have it. But I do submit that it is a misuse of federal power to enunciate a crop insurance scheme, placing 80 per cent of the financial responsibility outside the federal government, without at least the courtesy to have had prior consultation with the provincial governments. If anything is designed to wreck federal-provincial relations precipitously it is this kind of ill-considered action by this government.
The Saskatchewan government are anxious to bring any possible benefits to the people of that province that may accrue from crop insurance, but they resent very deeply the effort of the federal government to put most of the financial responsibility on the provinces, and they resent very deeply the callous disregard for normal federal-provincial relations and normal consultation.
The speech of the hon. member for Ros-thern is quite understandable. This is his bid to get back into the good graces of the party.
Shame.
We all know that he made a very interesting speech some days ago-
How low can you get?

-and that his speech came as a jolt, as a shock, to the government. In my memory of the house no government member has been more critical of government policy than was the hon. member for Rosthern in the speech he made.
What about the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska?
He might run a close second. But there are these two hon. members at any rate who have exposed the government's policy for exactly what it is. Apparently the pressure has been applied.
Oh, oh.

The hon. member now wishes to get back into the good graces of his party and so he is making this effort to restore his position. I think his independence has been very much a flash in the pan and that it will soon be forgotten because we now have this speech seeking readmission to the caucus of his party. He is asking for reinstatement and this is the speech of apology to the Minister of Agriculture.
The hon. member is talking nonsense.

It is the truth. That is why we are getting all these interruptions. However, I am hopeful that the hon. member for Rosthern will reread his correspondence from the prairies and will reread the speech

that he made in this house some days ago which was in much better perspective than was his speech today.
The item before the committee is one that will receive, I have no doubt, the unanimous support of hon. members. I have no doubt about that whatsoever,-
Then why are you talking?

-even though hon. gentlemen opposite may wish to interpret what we have said. With the hon. member for Timiskaming I should like to say that I feel that the reports made on the proceedings of this house could leave the wrong impression. I think the situation will be straightened out when this item, at an appropriate time, is passed-as I am certain it will be-unanimously by the committee.
May I correct an impression that was left by the hon. member for Assiniboia before we leave the matter?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: You mean you are still with us?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I recognize the hon. member for Rosthern.

I should like to say that the hon. member for Assiniboia has tried to leave a wrong impression. I cannot let pass any implication that I ever fell from grace in the party in which I consider myself one member. I want to assure him that anything I said today or said at any other time I will say in this house as the member for Rosthern and as the Conservative member for the constituency of Rosthern.

I think I should correct at this time some very incorrect statements which the hon. member for Assiniboia made. He asserted that the dominion government was reluctant to act to provide assistance for the farmers whose crops were covered by the snow. This statement is the very reverse of the truth. As soon as the early snow came we began to collect information immediately with the idea in mind of determining what steps would be necessary in order to provide some form of assistance to the farmers. To state that we were most reluctant to act is, I think, the complete reverse of the facts in connection with the matter and I am surprised that the hon. member would make that statement in view of the fact that I think he knows we began to move immediately after the snow came on.
But it took you so long to move.
You refused the submission that was made.

Another statement made by the hon. member for Assiniboia was that the dominion government made the announcement of what assistance would be available and the provinces could either take it or leave it. He went on from there to discuss crop insurance and to say that we had not consulted the provinces and so on. As far as this matter is concerned, the announcement which was made by the dominion government was made only after weeks of consultation with the provinces with regard to the form of assistance which would be provided and in an attempt to get the provinces to agree to the form of assistance which would be provided.
The hon. member for Timiskaming said, "You took weeks to do it". One of the reasons that it took weeks to get the form of assistance in operation was the length of time that we took in consultation with the provinces in order to try to work out something mutually satisfactory in the way of assistance. In other words, the idea that we just made an announcement and said to the provinces "Take it or leave it" is also directly the contrary of the facts. I say that we spent weeks in consultation with them in an attempt to arrive at a mutually satisfactory formula of assistance.
I wonder whether I might ask a question?
Yes.
Is the minister saying that when the announcement was made agreement had been obtained at that time?
No; I am not saying that.
No; of course not.

The hon. member is talking about reluctance. The reluctance in connection with this matter did not come from the dominion government. We were unable to get the provinces to agree to a formula of assistance, so eventually we announced what we, as a dominion government, were willing to do in connection with the matter. That was the only step-
That is exactly what I said.

-we had left open to us.
I thought I should correct those two statements at this time and not allow them to remain on the record uncontradicted. Had I allowed them to remain uncontradicted, the hon. member would probably say that as they were not contradicted, they must be true.

Perhaps this item would have been passed by now if there had not been some statements made by hon. gentlemen opposite earlier this afternoon. Of course,
Supply-Agriculture
they have the right to make those statements. But when those statements create a false impression as to the attitude of the opposition we have a similar right to correct that false impression. Incidentally, Mr. Chairman, when in the course of the statements that have been made, personal attacks were made on my friend the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, if a member on this side of the house takes exception of that kind of tactic and replies, I think he should not be subjected to the cries that were raised this afternoon, "How low can you get". The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate does not need any defence from me. But it is surely in order for us on this side to take exception to statements of that kind which are made, when they are made, without the kind of interruptions that we had when that was done this afternoon.
The position of our party in this matter has been made quite clear and it leaves no room for misrepresentation or misunderstanding. We have said from the beginning that we were in favour of this estimate. Indeed, the position we have taken is that weeks ago

two or three weeks ago-this should have been done by legislation, in which case the amount would have been made effective by now. But we can be in favour of this act or strongly opposed to the way in which it has been dealt with. Indeed, if the way we recommended it should be done had been followed by the government, the action would have been taken by now. That is surely an answer to the criticism that we are delaying the legislation.
It is also interesting to hear hon. members opposite depreciate the attention we are giving to procedure with regard to this matter. It was only Saturday night that the Prime Minister, in a speech in this city, talked about the restoration of the rights of parliament. It was not very long before that when some hon. members sitting on the opposite side of the house were very vociferous on every possible occasion when they thought the rights of parliament were being violated in respect of any kind of procedure.
We on this side feel that this is not the right procedure to have followed in this matter. We are being asked through this item in the estimates-and incidentally, it was not the procedure followed in 1951, as stated by the hon. member for Bow River- to vote $6 million to be spent on conditions prescribed by order in council. This, Mr. Chairman, from a government headed by a Prime Minister who not very long ago never lost an opportunity, and indeed was very expert in creating opportunities, to denounce in strong language what he used to call

Supply-Agriculture
government by order in council. This particular item reads, as was pointed out last Friday, "to authorize, in accordance with terms and conditions prescribed by the governor in Council", which, on the face of it, was an indication that some order in council must have already been passed. When that question was asked by my hon. friend for Kenora-Rainy River of the minister, as reported on page 793 of last Friday's Hansard, he was told to look it up. Then later the minister got up in the house and corrected himself, and apologized to the committee for having made a mistake; none had been passed. But the word is "prescribed", and we are entitled to take from that wording that an order in council has been passed. It is very surprising indeed that the minister concerned with the estimates did not know what the situation was at that time but had to find out later.
Parliament, then, is being asked to give a blank cheque for $8 million, and the government is later to write the conditions for spending this money by order in council. We ask what agreement, what arrangement, what assurance-whatever word you wish to use- has been reached with the provinces, presumably laying down the conditions under which this money is to be spent, but we cannot find out.
The minister said a few moments ago that there were weeks-I think he said weeks- of consultation and correspondence. He said in reply to the hon. member for Assiniboia that it was quite wrong to say the government was reluctant to act, because they had been in touch with the provinces from the very beginning, as soon as the emergency occurred. Then one of my hon. friends to my left said how wonderful it was for the members of the government, including the Prime Minister, to show they were aware of this emergency. If the government has had this contact and consultation and correspondence with the provinces, why cannot we get it?
Last Tuesday the Minister of Agriculture was asked to produce the correspondence. An order of the house to that effect was passed on Wednesday. A request for it was made again on Thursday so that we would have this correspondence before us when discussing this estimate.
It was put on the order paper the opening day.

Yes. Now, a week after, we are asked to pass an estimate of $6 million without this information before us. I know that the minister has said that he has not been able to get the consent of the provinces to the tabling of this correspondence. But the minister knows perfectly well-he has had a

lot of experience with provincial correspondence-that a request by telephone last week would hardly have been refused by any of the provincial governments concerned who are getting help under this estimate and in whose interest it would be to get the estimate through as quickly as possible. No doubt the provincial governments would recognize, even if this government does not, that it is the right of this parliament to know exactly for what this money is being voted and how it will be spent as a result of any assurance, agreement, contract, or whatever you wish to call it, with any provincial government.
I would ask the minister now before the estimate goes through if he has that correspondence? Can he tell us what is in it? Will he table it? Will he let us know the conditions involved in the correspondence, because this is an item to be passed by parliament but to be spent under conditions laid down by order in council. Are we not entitled to know, so far as any correspondence from the provinces can make it clear, what the conditions are to be? When we bring this matter up in this way, surely we are not to be accused of delaying the estimate, of showing our unwillingness to let this go through, or of being opposed to the substance of the matter because we are standing up for proper procedure and the rights of parliament in this matter.
So, Mr. Chairman, we reiterate our approval of the principle involved in this estimate. However, I would like to say, although perhaps the minister dealt with this in previous discussions when I was not here, and if so I apologize for mentioning it, that it seems to me to be a pretty rigid kind of provision when you get help if you qualify by reaching the 50 per cent mark, but if you have 49.5 per cent of your acreage under snow you do not qualify. Might it not have been more effective, and more desirable in every way, if there had been a kind of sliding scale of acreage qualification worked out? I do not know whether this has been dealt with or not. However, it is an important technical point.
As I say, Mr. Chairman, we are in favour of the principle and want to see the farmers helped in this emergency; but we protest the way it has been done. If our suggestion at the beginning of this session had been followed, this amount would have been voted by now and would have been available to the governments concerned.

Mr. Chairman, I must protest once more at the Leader of the Opposition setting up this straw man and knocking him down again, and suggesting that there has

been any disregard of parliament, that the procedure has not been correct, and so on and so forth. I have gone over this thing half a dozen times now and explained exactly what was done. I have pointed out it is exactly the same procedure as has been followed in the past with matters of this kind.

We do not accept that
statement.

This constant reiteration
on the part of hon. members of the opposition that the procedure which has been followed shows a disregard of parliament just will not stand up.
The Leader of the Opposition said that this was not the procedure which was followed in 1951 when there was a similar disaster of snow-covered crops. It certainly was not the procedure followed then, because in 1951 the Liberal government of which he was a part gave no assistance whatsoever, so naturally it was not the same procedure. They refused to give any assistance-
May I ask the minister a question. Does he realize that one of his colleagues on this side just stated as part of his argument that it was exactly the same procedure as followed in 1951.

I did not hear any colleague of mine make any such statement. The fact is, which I think the hon. member on reflection will admit, that in 1951 the government of which he was a part refused to give any assistance.
Not true.

What assistance did they
give?
Guaranteed loans by legislation.

They provided for bank
loans, the same type of thing which we put through the house the other day and which we indicated would be of very limited value.

You said "no assistance".
You should withdraw that.
You gave no cash assistance, not one nickel's worth.
Now you are changing it.

The Leader of the Opposition also stated that parliament has been asked to give a blank cheque, and he went on to say that the minister should let them know what the conditions are, and so on and so forth. I have let the committee know. On Friday last I gave in detail what the situation was, how it had come about, and exactly what were the assurances which
Supply-A griculture
we gave to the provinces. They were very, very simple indeed. They were that the dominion government, if parliament approved of course, would pay half the cost of assistance up to a maximum of $3 an acre for a maximum of 200 acres if a farmer's crop was 50 per cent or more under the snow. That was the case with cereal crops. For non-cereal crops we would pay up to a maximum of $600 a farmer. They were the only terms which we ever laid down. They are the terms embraced in the item which is before the house, and it was then at the discretion of the provinces to put in the type of scheme which they wanted in each particular case. As I pointed out last Friday, there was a different type of assistance scheme put in in each of the three prairie provinces.
The Leader of the Opposition started out by complaining about the cut-off at 50 per cent. He said it would have been better if this had been put on a sliding scale and so forth. But there was nothing to prevent a province putting it on a sliding scale if it wished to, and, in fact, in Saskatchewan, for example, they have put it on a sliding scale and there are 20 different categories of payments.
That is if over 50 per cent unthreshed.
Payments ranging from $3 an acre down to 20 cents, and I put a table on record in Hansard to show what these categories are.
The Leader of the Opposition was speaking of under 50 per cent.
He did not know what he was talking about.
Government arrogance.

In the other two provinces, Alberta and Manitoba, they have put in categories of $3 payments and $2 payments depending on how much grain each farmer had threshed. I do not think anything more needs to be said with regard to these various allegations-and that is all they are-there is nothing to support them-made by hon. members opposite that there has in some way been a disregard for parliament. This is a perfectly normal and legitimate way of achieving this object and all the precedents of the past support it as a means of dealing with a matter of this kind.
The Minister of Agriculture is wont when he finds himself in a difficult position to assume that he alone in this house has any knowledge of the problem under discussion.

Do not judge me by yourself.

Supply-Agriculture
In other words, the Minister of Agriculture is the only man in this house who knows anything about agriculture.
Hear, hear.

Now we have confirmation of that from some of the minister's own supporters. The Minister of Agriculture is the only man sitting on either the government or the opposition benches who knows anything about the problem of agriculture. And what is the proof of that? The minister himself has said so: I am the only man who knows anything about agriculture-

On a point of order, I ask the hon. member to point out any place in Hansard or any place in a press statement reporting a speech of mine where I have ever said any such thing. I have never made any such statement. It is the last statement I would ever make, and the hon. member, I think, knows it.

This last act of humility on the part of the minister has a persuasive effect. If it were not for the fact that I think the point still should be made I would not ask him to consider his observation of a few minutes ago when he said in answer to an interjection of mine: "The Leader of the Opposition does not know what he is talking about."
Correct.

That is the reply which the hon. gentleman makes at every point. I wonder if it was the kind of reply he wanted to make when the former independent member from Rosthern made the very courageous and constructive observation that he did on the government's change of agricultural policy from one of price support to one of deficiency payments. The Minister of Agriculture ought to realize at the beginning of the session, since he is going to be piloting a number of measures, that one of the effective ways of getting legislation through is by some condescension, some expression of humility; a little acknowledgment that there might be a scintilla of knowledge of the subject on benches other than the one he himself occupies. That, I believe, the minister would find an effective way of dealing with the question in hand.
On a point of order, I fail to see what relation the remarks of the hon. member for Essex East bear to item 613 of the estimates.
You wouldn't see it.

I agree that there is not too much relevancy in what I have been saying to the point at issue, but there

is as much relevancy as the unwise remark of the minister that the Leader of the Opposition does not know what he is talking about. What I am trying to do now for the benefit of the experienced member for Springfield who has just intervened is to indicate that if the Minister of Agriculture wants to make some progress in the passage of measures which concern him he ought to develop a quality which is really characteristic of him, particularly when he was sitting on this side, and that is a little humility. After all, when the minister is playing golf he shows understanding and good fellowship; he understands the position of others. He should not let the fact that he has become Minister of Agriculture to so affect him. After all, it is not worth it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: You are off the fairway now.

The Leader of the Opposition has made some important points, and the Minister of Agriculture has not dealt with two of them. The Leader of the Opposition asked whether in respect of legislation which everyone in this house supports consideration was given by the federal government or by any one of the three provinces to giving assistance to farmers whose crops were under snow in respect of an amount less than 50 per cent. The Minister of Agriculture misunderstood the point made by the Leader of the Opposition. The Leader of the Opposition recognized that some provinces, notably Saskatchewan, did make provision on a graduated scale with regard to that portion of the crop which was under snow but which was over 50 per cent. The point made by the Leader of the Opposition was this: could consideration not be given to the case of an individual whose crops were, let us say, less than 50 per cent under the snow, but which had suffered considerable damage? Suppose the percentage was 49.5? To that question the minister did not address himself.
There is another point to which I think the Minister of Labour should have his attention directed, and it is this-
You are mixed up in your portfolio.

I was just anticipating that the Minister of Labour and I, once this measure has been dealt with, have some questions to discuss. That is undoubtedly what was in my mind. I am now saying to the Minister of Agriculture: what you are doing now is providing by way of an estimate for a group of farmers in this country who need assistance. The hon. member for Rosthern was guilty of a terminological inexactitude when he said that we on

this side of the house, by indicating that there were other classes of farmers in the country who needed assistance, were thereby attaching a condition to our approval of this measure. Nothing of that sort was stated in this house by any member of the Liberal party or in any other section of the chamber, and I have followed every bit of this debate.
What the Minister of Agriculture has failed to do is to answer the question of the Leader of the Opposition: if we are not to be given the right to deal with this matter by way of legislation in the usual form, by way of a bill on which a wide measure of discussion is permitted on the preamble and on the first clause, then, surely, we should have been furnished by the Minister of Agriculture with an opportunity of perusing the correspondence between the two governments concerned. The order was passed on Wednesday, as the Leader of the Opposition pointed out. There was nothing to prevent an active minister of labour who knows everything about agriculture-
The Minister of Labour hastens to confess that he knows nothing about agriculture.

-having one of his officials contact one of the ministers concerned in the provinces so we could now determine whether or not this legislation is considered by provincial governments who are paying 50 per cent to be a measure which fully meets the situation. For this government through the Minister of Agriculture to not be in a position of being able to put this correspondence on the table of the house when the motion ordering the production of these documents appeared on the order paper the first day is to reveal nothing less than a real indication of this government's contempt for the rights of parliament.
Oh, oh.

My hon. friend the learned member from an Edmonton constituency whose contributions this session have consisted of groans and that kind of intervention knows perfectly well that it is contemptuous of any government toward parliament to refuse to bring down correspondence that has such relevancy to an item such as that under discussion, and that from a government that continually prides itself on being the champion of the rights of the people and of parliament.
I regret that the Minister of Agriculture who does not understand these things concerning the rights of parliament apparently should be the instrument in this particular
Supply-A griculture
instance of this further disregard by the government of the rights of the representatives of the people. That is understandable in the case of a man who, as he says, knows everything about agriculture.
Mr. Chairman-
Mr. Chairman-

The hon. member for Essex East from that pinnacle of wisdom that he takes for granted he has reached loves to lecture the House of Commons and the members in it as to what they should and should not do. He has just given us a demonstration of that. After lecturing me for some considerable time he managed to lecture two or three other hon. members of the committee during the course of the few short remarks he has just made. I know it tickles his vanity to assume this Olympian attitude and to deliver these lectures but I do not think many people in this chamber pay them as much attention as the hon. member for Essex East thinks they deserve.
In addition to soothing his vanity and delivering his lectures the only thing the hon. member accomplished in his remarks was to reiterate the matter of disregard for parliament. I do not propose to repeat time after time what I have already said on the subject which I believe demonstrates as clearly as it can be demonstrated that there has been absolutely no disregard for parliament in the conduct of the government.
Although the hon. member for Essex East has implied that 1 am not in a position to recognize disregard for parliament I should like to point out that my record in that regard is much better than his or those of the hon. gentlemen who sit with him who were members of the previous government and who distinguished themselves in the last parliament in which they were in office by their utter disregard of parliament particularly during the pipe line debate.
Blank cheque legislation here.

All of this, Mr. Chairman,
I must confess is completely out of order as far as discussion of this estimate is concerned and therefore I do not intend to pursue these matters further.

Mr. Chairman, before the minister sits down will he deal with the two points raised, one being the correspondence which he refuses to table and the other the question of the sliding scale which might take into consideration percentages below 50? He has not dealt with either.

Mr. Chairman, I dealt with the second point before when I mentioned

Supply-Agriculture

speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. S-8, respecting the British and Foreign Bible Society in Canada.

maintopic: THE BRITISH AND FOREIGN BIBLE SOCIETY IN CANADA
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: THE BRITISH AND FOREIGN BIBLE SOCIETY IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in presenting this bill perhaps the house may be interested to learn that the British and Foreign Bible Society was founded on March 7, 1804, at a public meeting held in the London tavern, 123 Bishopsgate street, London. Its sole object was to encourage the wider circulation of the scriptures without note or comment. Its first foreign translation was for Canada, a Mohawk-English gospel of St. John, translated by Captain Norton, chief of the Six Nation Indians in Upper Canada.
From that beginning in Canada this society spread from east to west until 1904 when it was decided that the various auxiliaries throughout Canada should federate and form a national society. Royal assent to the act of incorporation was given on March 22, 1906, the reference being chapter 74 of the statutes of Canada of 1906. This act was amended from time to time. On May 30, 1930 royal assent was given to one amending act. Also at the time of the entry of Newfoundland into confederation a further amendment was made.
One purpose of this amendment to the present act is to change the name of the society from "The British and Foreign Bible Society in Canada" to "Canadian Bible Society, Auxiliary of The British and Foreign Bible Society". The British and Foreign Bible Society in Canada is the national bible society for Canada and one of the 23 national bible societies in the world. The present name conveys the impression that the society is a British society and a foreign society and therefore not primarily a Canadian responsibility. The new name will designate the society as a Canadian society in a way in which the present bill does not designate it and it will also preserve the close and intimate links with the parent society.
Another purpose of the bill is to make possible the appointment of certain prominent Canadians to the general board, with the provision that the majority of the members shall be elected by the auxiliaries or districts. The society feel that this provision will enable them to obtain greater representation on the general board of their society.
The act, of course, also restates the objects of the society but there is no real change in the purpose of the society. It also changes
[The Deputy Chairman.]

the limitation that presently is on the society in respect of holding property. I believe the amendment in 1930 raised the limitation to $1 million. I understand the limitation in the original act was $20,000. This time they are asking that no limitation be put on the value of real estate which might be held by this society.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I would suggest to the house that the amendment is quite in order. When this bill is referred to the appropriate committee the officers of the society together will the legal representative of the society will be present to answer any questions hon. gentlemen might have.

Mr. Speaker, before making a few brief remarks on the bill respecting the flag of Canada, let me read the explanatory note that appears in the printed bill.
As it is desirable and urgent that Canada possess a distinctive national flag, this bill provides a method of obtaining a flag with the least possible delay. The method adopted is to have the governor in council prepare the design immediately upon the passage of this bill and to submit the design for approval to the house and the other place at this session. In this manner Canadians could have a distinctive national flag at the end of this session.
Mr. Speaker, I will make only a few remarks on this bill, so that I will not prolong the debate and risk having Bill C-14 buried under a mound of flowers.
Mr. Speaker, may I say that, strange as it may seem, we know in advance that hon. members opposite will rise in praise of such a bill and take a long time-unfortunately too much time-to say they are absolutely
Flags of Canada
in favour of a truly Canadian flag without any symbol reminiscent of colonialism or of our subservience to European countries.
Let me point out that one of the members who dealt recently with this problem of our flag was the hon. member for Ottawa East (Mr. Richard), who has long advocated a distinctive national flag. I wholeheartedly support his request for a truly Canadian flag for the 100th anniversary of confederation. However, Mr. Speaker, I want to be even more optimistic than the hon. member for Ottawa East. I believe that we should have a national emblem long before that. Why not this very year?
Long before our centenary as a young country, we should prove in the face of the world that we are now an adult nation, that we have reached maturity, and that for quite some time now, we have had no need of tutelage by European countries. That should be shown on our flag, and the matter is urgent.
At a time when Canada is growing increasingly popular throughout the world, it is almost an insult for us not to have either a distinctive flag or a distinctive national hymn.
So it is that, at times, even now Europeans, Americans, Asiatics and other people look upon Canada as a colony.
Our national pride should at last be aroused and make us take concrete, realistic and truly Canadian action. After all, Mr. Speaker, we are adults, and we must prove it without delay.
Public opinion polls show that Canadians tend to accept a purely distinctive emblem with growing enthusiasm. This is more obvious among the younger people born and educated in this country.
A few years ago, the leader of the C.C.F., Mr. M. J. "In their pride, they would cut out a piece of cotton and draw a maple leaf on it," said Mr. Coldwell.
Whether our future flag includes a maple leaf or not, it is not my personal problem. What counts is that we should have a flag of our own as soon as possible.
Mr. Speaker, I shall not reiterate the brilliant speeches on that matter that have been made through the years. I only want

to beg our friends opposite to tell us as briefly as possible, whether or not they favour the distinctive national flag bill.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR A NATIONAL FLAG OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to participate in this debate on Bill C-14, concerning the adoption of a distinctive national flag, as introduced by the hon. member for Drum-mond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger). I am prepared to admit that, if the hon. member had been a member of the House of Commons under the former administration, he would have introduced a similar bill with the same sincerity. However, I shall not dwell on the omissions and inaction of the former administration, because we could discuss this matter for hours without ever reaching any agreement.
Mr. Speaker, the adoption of a distinctive national flag is a matter of too much importance to make it a political or party affair. There is no doubt that the majority of Canadians now favour the adoption of a distinctive national flag, one that would include no other flag nor any other symbol of some other country.
For many years, we have been receiving folders and letters from all parts of Canada, including resolutions recommending certain flag designs. Most of those resolutions favour the adoption of this or that design, one which includes the union jack, or one bearing some distinctive symbol such as the maple leaf. However, I am of the opinion that the pleas of a large proportion of Canadians for inclusion of the union jack should be seriously considered, even if we are not bound to share that opinion.
In this regard I should like to quote part of a resolution sent in to us by the Supreme Bodge of the Sons of England Benefit Society: (Text):
At a meeting of the Supreme Council of the Sons of England Benefit Society, held in the Sons of England building, Toronto, on May 1, 1959, the following motion was presented and approved. Moved, W. J. Phillips, seconded, H. Pickering:
Be it resolved, that the Supreme Council of the Sons of England Benefit Society request the government of Canada to retain the union jack as part of any Canadian flag which may be approved or adopted by the said parliament.
(Translation):
It will be seen, Mr. Speaker, that those people want us to keep the union jack on our flag. About this, Mr. Speaker, I should like

to express my personal opinion, even if it is not original. I believe there is something to be said for the idea expressed by a Canadian citizen, now a senator, that the union jack is too fine a flag to be demeaned into an accessory symbol on some other flag.
I have here another folder received from an association known as the National Council of the Native Sons of Canada which, through Mr. Eugene Collins, a lawyer in Calgary, submitted a brief on this matter. Here is a summary of the opinion held by that group:
(Text):
A flag which included the union jack would tend to suppress our individuality, while a flag excluding it and built around the maple leaf would tend to stress that individuality. The flag with the union jack has failed to inspire the maximum affinity between Canadians of all ethnic origins while the maple leaf would serve such a function with much greater effectiveness.
(Translation):
That, Mr. Speaker, is the opinion of a group of Alberta citizens.
Polls which have been taken recently on the matter, both by crown corporations and by independent firms, have quite definitely indicated that a strong majority of Canadians want a distinctive flag.
Personally, I think it is time that Canada should have a distinctive national emblem.

Mr. Speaker,
I sincerely admire the patriotism of the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger). Indeed, I can only regret that so much patriotism failed to inspire the Liberal party at the time it was administering the country. This would have spared the sponsor of this bill the need to resort to a political stratagem to arouse public opinion once again and attempt to start quarrels that are always bitter and fruitless.
