Mr. Chairman, I think we will all welcome the information which has just been given to the committee by the Minister of Agriculture. It comes rather late in a long, drawn-out debate. The minister will realize that it would be impossible while the debate continues for any member of the opposition to have an opportunity of perusing adequately the correspondence that he has in mind. But I do see a merit in this, that up to now we have all had the feeling that the minister was unnecessarily reticent about even his discussions with the provinces with respect to this matter, and I assume that while in a practical way it may be very difficult for us to become familiar with the correspondence, at least with respect to two provinces out of three the Minister of Agriculture will now feel it possible to discuss with other hon. members of the committee some matters that are probably referred to in the correspondence.
I want to give the committee a few illustrations of the impossible situation we were put in without our being able to consider the correspondence and the communications between the provinces and the federal government with respect to this important matter. This afternoon the minister, I think in reply to a question from the Leader of the Opposition with respect to opportunities for some form of graduated assistance for those who had unthreshed crops which were less than 50 per cent, made the statement, which I do not think has been clarified, that the provinces were free in the area under 50 per cent down to zero of unthreshed grain. It was not made clear, but I think the Minister of Agriculture will agree that what he was suggesting was that, in respect of unthreshed grain to a degree between zero and 50 per cent, he was anticipating that in that category the provinces were free, but they were free simply to go ahead and do something 100 per cent at their own cost. Am I not right in thinking that the federal government stipulated that its assistance would only be provided with respect to unthreshed grain over 50 per cent?
The other point that I was curious about this afternoon was this relationship between entitlement under the Prairie Farm

Supply-Agriculture
Assistance Act and entitlement for assistance under the proposition which is before us in this estimate. I find that on February 2 there is a report in the Winnipeg Tribune saying that questions were being raised in the Manitoba legislature as to whether or not persons who were eligible for Prairie Farm Assistance Act payments would be eligible to receive assistance under this assistance scheme shared equally between the provinces and the federal government. I assume that the correspondence will have something to say as to the decisions made in each of these three provinces with respect to this particular qualification.
I hope the minister will perhaps now give more information to the house on this point. Would he tell us whether or not it was a federal stipulation that payments would not be made on the two accounts, or whether this was open entirely to the provinces to make a decision, and which provinces did actually decide that any one that received anything under P.F.A.A. would be disentitled to a payment under this scheme. Alternatively, would he tell us whether or not they were not entirely disentitled but perhaps would have their payment under this scheme discounted by the amount of any payments under P.F.A.A.

Mr. Chairman, if the hon. member will read Hansard for Friday last he will see I made it very plain indeed that the only conditions that we laid down in regard to this matter were the ones I mentioned earlier here today as well as on Friday. No mention was made in any way in connection with P.F.A.A. payments. As a matter of fact, I pointed out to the provinces that the Prairie Farm Assistance Act stands on its own feet and that under that act any farmer who is in a township which is entitled to payment will be paid, and must be paid, under the P.F.A. act. We as the dominion government at no time made any stipulation in regard to P.F.A.A. payments. I stated that on Friday last as clearly as I have now stated it here.
I recall that, but I ask the minister whether or not the correspondence which we have not yet before us indicates what, for example, was the decision made in the province of Manitoba in that respect?

Mr. Chairman, hon. members opposite, I think, will be very disappointed in this correspondence. The amount of correspondence is not great to begin with, because most of these discussions were carried on at actual conferences and by means of the telephone. Therefore the amount of

correspondence is not extensive. The particular point which the hon. member brings up comes into the correspondence only to a very limited extent in the form of requests or queries as to whether P.F.A.A. payments should be made or not.

Is the minister unaware of what stipulations are being put into force under the regulations in Manitoba in this respect? Because I find that the lack of adequate information, not only in a provincial legislature, but up to now here, has caused a fair amount of parliamentary confusion. In the article which I read I found that in the Manitoba legislature the minister of agriculture was asked whether or not the responsibility for deciding that entitlement under P.F.A.A. would disqualify payments under the assistance scheme was a provincial decision. The speaker there ruled that it had nothing to do with the provincial legislature, and consequently the matter could not be a subject for a question to the provincial minister of agriculture.
I am asking the federal Minister of Agriculture what he knows and can tell the committee about the rules in Manitoba in the relationship of P.F.A.A. payments to payments under this assistance scheme.

Mr. Chairman, I have
already stated the only stipulations which the dominion government put in as far as these particular assistance payments are concerned. Therefore, it must be clear to the hon. member and to every other hon. member of this committee that whatever restrictions were put in with regard to P.F.A.A. payments and these assistance payments were not put in by the dominion government.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think that is the point that the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River is making at all. We are asked in this parliament to pay 50 per cent of the cost of these payments in the three provinces. Surely, when we are called upon to vote money to pay half the cost we are entitled to know the condition under which these payments are being made by the government of Manitoba. That is what my hon. friend is asking. We want to know precisely what these conditions are.
Mr. Chairman, I should like now to table the correspondence with Alberta and Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The usual procedure in
committee, is, I believe, to file it with the Clerk.

Thank you. In connection with the point which has been raised, may I say that the particular type of scheme put

into effect in each province was the responsibility of that province. The province took responsibility for it and is in each case administering the scheme and putting it into effect. As far as the dominion government is concerned, we said we would pay half the cost of making a payment of $3 an acre to any farmer who has less than 50 per cent of his crop threshed up to a maximum of 200 acres, which comes to $600. And we would pay half the cost up to the same amount for people with special problems. Those were the only stipulations we laid down, and what stipulations any particular province puts into effect are its own business. As long as the provinces do not make payments in excess of what we said we would pay half there will be no difficulty. As a matter of fact in practically all cases-perhaps I had better say in a very large number of cases, particularly in Saskatchewan-the payments made are less than the amounts of which we offered to pay half, and surely that is the only thing with which this parliament is concerned.

These payments are being made to Canadian citizens by Canadian taxpayers and surely we are entitled to know precisely the conditions under which these payments are being made. It is most unreasonable to ask us to vote this money without the knowledge which any person who has any sense of his responsibility to the taxpayers of this country and any sense of his responsibility to the electorate is entitled to have. Surely this government did not tell the provinces: you can pick farmer A and exclude farmer B but we will still pay 50 per cent even under the most arbitrary scheme possible. It is impossible for me to believe that any government would be so irresponsible as not to know the basis on which these payments are being made. What we want to know are the terms and conditions under which the Manitoba government is making these payments, payments of which we are being asked to pay half.

I do not think the little political speech we have just heard from the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate bears on the matter at all. I think I put the situation very clearly when I spoke a moment ago. We have not attempted to dictate to the provinces as to the type of scheme they should have. That is what the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate with his usual authoritarian point of view thinks we should have done. We did not do that. It has been the responsibility of each province to devise the type of scheme which it wished to put into operation within the general conditions we laid down. The schemes are the responsibility of the provinces concerned. They are 79951-0-57J
Supply-Agriculture
receiving the applications, carrying out the inspections and making the payments. When they have done this they will bill us for half the cost. We will examine the accounts and make sure they have stayed within the limits we have laid down. And so long as they have done that, we will pay half the cost of the payments they have made. I do not think anything could be simpler than that.
As far as the actual details of the schemes put into effect in the three provinces are concerned, the information which I received from the provinces was in the form of press releases which they put out in each case. It just so happens I have not got them with me at the moment, but I have sent for them and expect them to be here in a few minutes.

I might remind the minister that the authoritarian government to which I belonged did have a number of schemes involving payment of 50 per cent of the cost of provincial measures-the old age assistance program, for instance-but my hon. friend from Essex East had enough sense of responsibility to the treasury to know the conditions under which the provinces made these payments, and those conditions were ratified by this parliament before one nickel went out of the treasury. I have not the least doubt that the hon. member who succeeded my hon. friend from Essex East, the hon. member for Perth who is now Minister of National Health and Welfare, is also insistent on knowing these things, because he told this house so in the case of hospital insurance and in the case of the changes which were made in the unemployment assistance provisions. In every case in my knowledge in which 50 per cent was paid, we have known in this parliament, and been told, the precise conditions under which the money was made available.
The Minister of Agriculture can put words in my mouth if he likes, but I did not say he should have dictated the terms. I said he should know the terms. We who have to vote this money and who were elected to look after the treasury are entitled to know these things and all I am asking now is that the hon. gentleman should tell us what are the terms under which we are voting this money.
Order.

Is it not a fact that the information which the hon. member requests is already on record in Hansard and was put on Hansard at page 781 beginning in the middle of the page, where it says: "The program in Manitoba is as follows" and lists the circumstances under which the payments are being made in that province?

Supply-Agriculture
The hon. gentleman, who claims to be a spokesman for Manitoba, has not shown the interest even to read Hansard or to pay any attention when other hon. members are speaking to this item. It seems to me that members of the opposition want the government to instruct them not only on what the policy of this government is with regard to these payments but also on the policies of all the provincial governments. That policy is on record and it is available for members of the opposition to find. If they wish they may obtain it from the newspapers or through their colleagues in the Manitoba legislature who are putting up the same kind of obstructionism as we are witnessing here today. If members of the opposition do not know more about agriculture than to talk around the subject, it is about time they sat and listened.

I feel that this is a good measure and one which will put a lot of money into the hands of farmers whose crops are under the snow. I have many farmers in my constituency who are facing this experience. I will say that I also have some farmers in fringe areas who are going to have a difficult time getting paid under this program. We must admit that under any legislation which may be introduced it will be hard to see that everybody is paid.
I am sure that this government will bring in some legislation to help out the farmers who have not been assisted by this program.
Of all those who have participated in the debate today I am the only farmer who has risen to speak. By farmer I mean a man who lives on his farm and operates it. That is what I do. I saw the snow fall on 300 acres of my crops last fall and on my neighbours' crops. I did not sit back and wait for somebody to come to my assistance. I immediately phoned the Minister of Agriculture and told him that disaster had struck our part of the country.
What have we witnessed in this chamber during the discussion of this estimate over the course of the last few days? We have seen the farm expert, the hon. member for Essex East, and another distinguished farm expert, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, rise in their places and speak at length. In my submission the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate does not know a head of wheat from the tail end of a codfish. Both he and the hon. member for Essex East wasted the time of the committee with political manoeuvring.
We have also seen the hon. member for Assiniboia, who in this chamber is up and down and up and down wasting the time of the committee and has been doing it for 16 years. I got tired of listening to him and

said, "That is C.C.F. trash". The hon. member said, "Oh, do you mean to say that you call the Western Producer trash?" I maintain that I called his speech C.C.F. trash.
Let us examine what the Western Producer has said on the subject. An article entitled "Emergency Disaster Fund Asked by SFU" reads as follows:
The Saskatchewan government should establish a $10 million disaster reserve fund which would serve to cushion provincial funds in any future distress problems that might affect any segment of the population, the Saskatchewan farmers union urged in its annual presentation to the provincial cabinet Dec. 29.
On Friday last my friend the hon. member for Assiniboia and my very good friend the hon. member for Essex East suggested that if these deficiency payments had been paid as requested by the farm delegation we would not need this relief measure today. Let me point out that I attended a meeting in my constituency of 120 farmers. The chairman rose and said that in 1957 we were hailed out, in 1958 we were dried out and in 1959 our crops lay under the snow. I ask these hon. gentlemen how these farmers would get a red cent out of these deficiency payments on a bushel basis? They would not get a five cent piece nor would many of the farmers I represent.
The hon. member for Assiniboia says that the farm organizations are the spokesmen of western Canada. I will agree that they probably are for the constituency of Assiniboia because the hon. member for that constituency is too busy travelling around eastern Canada organizing that new political party to attend to the needs of the farmers in his constituency. In my constituency I work in co-operation with the farm organizations. I came to parliament to speak for the farmers in my riding and that is what I am doing here tonight.
In the Winnipeg Free Press we saw a headline which read:	Are Prairie Farmers
Pampered? The article went on to deal with the suggestion that eastern members of parliament are of the opinion that the western farmers are getting too much money. I do not believe that of hon. members of this committee. I invite any hon. member in this chamber regardless of his party to stand up and say he is opposed to the farmers getting this money.
You see, Mr. Chairman, no one has stood up. Therefore, since we are all in agreement, I say that for two days we have wasted time witnessing something which amounts only to political manipulation. The opposition has taken the position in which it said: When you were over here you treated us like this so now we are going to treat you the same way.

I say that if we are all in agreement, as I am sure we are, it is time to close this debate and vote on this estimate so that the money will be passed on to the farmers of western Canada and this committee can get on with other important business. Surely this is what the people of Canada sent us here for, not to sit like a bunch of kids playing political games.

Mr. Chairman, I had hoped to ask a question of the hon. member for Springfield before he took his seat. After the reading he has undertaken of the Manitoba Hansard and the Hansard of this parliament, would he answer this question which was ruled out of order by a vote of the Manitoba legislature 32 to 18:	Why are
farmers eligible for P.F.A.A. not eligible for assistance under the provincial-federal emergency aid program?

Mr. Chairman, I do not think it is within the province of any hon. member of this committee to answer a question concerning why a question was ruled out of order in the Manitoba legislature. If the hon. member wants an answer to that question I think he should write a letter to the speaker of the Manitoba legislative assembly.

Mr. Chairman, I asserted that the question was overruled in the Manitoba legislature and I did not ask why it was overruled. The hon. member indicated that he had done a lot of homework in looking at provincial Hansards and the records of this house. I invited him to answer the question as to why farmers eligible for P.F.A.A. are not eligible for assistance under the provincial-federal emergency aid program. The question was ruled out of order in the Manitoba legislative assembly where it was considered not relevant but presumably it is relevant here because it refers to a federal statute.

Mr. Chairman, as the Minister of Agriculture has already said, I think rulings in the Manitoba legislative assembly are not for me to comment upon. However, what the hon. member was trying to drag in was the question of P.F.A.A. payments. Naturally the Manitoba legislature did not want to discuss those payments because they come under the jurisdiction of the federal government.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I would ask the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) to take a rest from the beautiful English language and to listen instead to the beautiful French language, though I do not speak it so well.
We are asked to vote an amount of $6 million. Needless to say, we are in favour
Supply-Agriculture
of voting these $6 million in order to help those who suffered from bad weather conditions in the three western provinces.
However, we find it strange that the Minister of Agriculture has given us no detailed account with regard to the amount of $6 million provided in this item. We are called upon to pass an item of $6 million, as we would be asked to vote $6.
I would like to know what portion will be paid to each of the three provinces. We would also like to know how many farmers, farms, and acres were affected by weather conditions. Moreover, as the federal government is paying this amount by request of the provinces, we would like to know who inspects the damaged areas. Moreover, we also would like to be informed whether the federal government, which will have to pay out $6 million, will send inspectors to check whether the people employed by the provinces are submitting accurate reports.
I believe we are entitled to receive this information because-as the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) said recently-we are asked to vote a sum of money for which arrangements have been made in advance. We are placed before a fait accompli. Those payments are practically promised and we are asked to vote an amount of $6 million without getting any detail.
I surely would like to know from the Mini-ister of Agriculture whether this government is relying exclusively on the authorities of the various provinces that will benefit from this amount of money, or whether he has, first of all, taken into consideration the interest of Canadians, in personally sending out inspectors to check whether the number of farms, the number of devastated acres have actually been inspected, and if, really, farmers are entitled to that amount of money we are asked to approve? Besides, that amount is perhaps inadequate.
We would also like to know whether, tomorrow or the next day, when other supplementary estimates are asked for, we might be asked to vote an additional amount for the same purpose.
Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member does not like this item very much.
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman.

No, I now have the floor, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, this interjection is out of order; it is a false argument. But, in reply to the question of the hon. member for St. Denis (Mr. Denis), I must say it is not possible at this moment to supply the specific amounts of that payment.
Mr. Chairman, I have here the estimated amounts for the three provinces, and I shall give them to the committee.
(Text):
These estimates of cost were made by the provinces. In the case of Manitoba, the payments to farmers amount to $1,200,000, administration costs, $50,000, benefiting farmers, 4,000; Saskatchewan, payments to farmers, $4,500,000, administration costs, $40,000, benefiting farmers, 15,000; Alberta, payments to farmers, $5,400,000, administration costs, $50,000, benefiting farmers, 18,000. This makes total payments to farmers of $11,100,000, administration costs, $140,000, for a total of $11,240,000, and benefiting farmers, 37,000.
As I attempted to say in my regrettable poor French-
It was good.

-it is absolutely impossible to estimate the total amount that would be required with any exactitude. However, the provinces have estimated that this is the probable amount of payment and, as a result, in order to pay half of this cost we have provided this estimate of $6 million, which will pay half of their estimates plus a certain amount more because it is likely there will be more people coming in during the later period than the provinces probably estimated.
May I ask the minister if he will answer my question? Did the federal officials inspect these premises or is the minister relying upon provincial inspectors?

The administration of the scheme, Mr. Chairman, is entirely in the hands of the provinces. As I said before, the accounts will be checked by officers of the dominion government, but the officials of the provincial government made the estimate as part of their administration of the scheme.

Mr. Chairman, as this debate goes on one becomes terribly confused. At this hour of 8.40 p.m. on Tuesday, February 9, I am not quite sure whether we are trying to give some relief to the western farmers who had crops snowed under last year or whether we are laying the basis for next year's disaster. This debate has revolved around two or three points. Last Thursday or Friday the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate made a great point of whether or not there was an agreement with the provinces before the agreement was signed by the federal government. Today he has had a great deal to say with respect to the production of papers.
I do not know too much about the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. I do not know whether he lives in Bonavista or Twillingate or Ottawa or Winnipeg or on a farm in Manitoba. He told us the other night he was raised on a farm and became partially emaciated. If he did, he has certainly made a remarkable recovery. I should like to say to him that mine is a very simple mind and when these tremendous problems arise I always try to reduce them to simple principles. I should like to say to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, to his colleagues and to my good friends in the far corner, if he were going to build a house he would certainly consult with a contractor and, if he had enough money and he probably has, an architect. Having decided upon the plan he was going to follow, he would probably call in a lawyer-perhaps he would not now- and he would draw up a contract.
This is what this government has done, Mr. Chairman. This whole discussion has been a waste of time. We had a situation in western Canada that required some discussion. Those discussions were held and a general principle was evolved by this government. I want to say to you, so far as I am concerned-let me add I know nothing about agriculture; I leave that to the hon. member for Essex East and the hon. member for Assiniboia-I feel that when the emergency arose the Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture became concerned. They held these conversations, and now we are drawing up the contract. I wonder what kind of a house my friend from Bonavista-Twillingate would obtain, when he becomes domiciled somewhere, if he did not follow that procedure?

So far as the production of papers is concerned, Mr. Chairman, that means very little to the western farmer. We have an emergency and we are trying to deal with it. The government has dealt with it on the best and most practical basis possible. For heaven's sake, let us get on, pass this appropriation and move on to something that may be more important to the whole Dominion of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, earlier in the proceedings I made the statement that the three prairie provinces were united in presenting a proposition to the government that differed from the action later taken. I suggested that in the correspondence exchanged between the federal government and the governments of the three prairie provinces would be found evidence that the action taken by the federal government was not in keeping with the requests that had been made and that there would likely be evidence damaging to the stand taken by the federal government.
The Minister of Agriculture denied that this was so and said that the correspondence contained nothing that would not be advantageous to the government. 1 believe he even went further in his denial with regard to the statement I had made. I have in my hand now the file of correspondence that was tabled a few moments ago. I want to congratulate the Minister of Agriculture on his excellent use of the French language and this further additional evidence of his efficiency on occasion in finding, between six o'clock and when we met again at eight o'clock or shortly thereafter, that he was able to produce the correspondence.
There are many letters exchanged in the file of correspondence but I want to refer to one in particular dated November 6, 1959. It is addressed to the minister and was sent to him weeks before the federal government's policy was made public. I wish to point out that this letter bears three signatures. I have seen a lot of correspondence tabled in the house from time to time consisting of exchanges between the federal government and various provincial governments but in my memory this is the first time a joint letter bearing the signatures of responsible cabinet ministers has been submitted by a number of provincial governments.
The letter is signed by G. H. Hutton, minister of agriculture for Manitoba, I. C. Nollet, minister of agriculture for Saskatchewan and L. C. Halmrast, minister of agriculture for Alberta. In the letter they set forth very clearly the policy that they wish the government to follow. The letter reads in part as follows:
Dear Mr. Harkness:
Following your telephone conversation with each of the ministers of agriculture of the three prairie
Supply-Agriculture
provinces, we met in Regina on November 6 to discuss the matters you raised, and the general feed and income situation. I should add that following your telephone conversation, each minister discussed the situation with his government and the following represents the viewpoints arrived at.
We agree that need must be the determining factor to the granting of financial assistance, but this requires that realized yield per specified acre be the basis upon which the award is calculated and financial assistance distributed. We also agreed that due to a most unusual phase of weather experienced this fall, the present situation was of the nature of a national emergency.
That is the first main point made by these representatives of the three prairie governments. The letter goes on:
The federal government, through passage of the P.F.A. Act in 1939, together with western farmer participation, accepted the responsibility of providing financial assistance to farmers suffering disastrous crop losses. The only difference between the current emergency and others suffered during the past 20 years is that farmers are now much less uniformly affected than they were, as for example, in drought years or during rust infestations. As a result a great many farmers in distress will be located in ineligible P.F.A.A. areas.
Therefore we propose that needy farmers who will not qualify for P.F.A.A. awards because they are not in eligible areas be dealt with individually and assistance be granted as of December 1 on the same basis as to those farmers who qualify under the provisions of the act. The foregoing proposal should not be considered an extension of P.F.A.A. but rather as an emergency measure.
We also request, as discussed at Winnipeg, that P.F.A.A. be authorized to consider all swathed or standing crops not threshed as at December 1 to be complete failures and P.F.A.A. awards to be made on this basis.
Here then is a proposal by the three prairie governments that this situation be considered a national emergency and that the Prairie Farm Assistance Act be modified so that farmers who have crops unthreshed may be eligible for prairie farm assistance. As hon. members know, the Prairie Farm Assistance Act is a charge on the federal government and not on the provincial treasuries. Therefore this proposal is in keeping with the statements I have made that the provinces were asking the federal government to assume this responsibility instead of doing what they have now done, that is place half of the responsibility on the provincial treasuries. I will omit two paragraphs of the letter having to do with specialized crops. The minister can put those on the record if he cares to do so. The letter then continues:
We discussed at length responsibilities which the provinces could reasonably be expected to assume in this emergency. First, it is inevitable that the conditions referred to will have a depressing affect on provincial revenues. Second, all provinces have undertaken to provide freight assistance on the movement of fodder and bedding on a shareable basis with your government and also on feed grains. Third, all .provinces expect to be required to render financial assistance to municipalities and unorganized districts for the purchase of feed and in providing seed grain, tractor fuels, etc., for

Supply-Agriculture
field operations in 1960. Furthermore, the need for public assistance or social aid will certainly be affected by these conditions.
For these reasons we consider that provinces cannot reasonably be expected to assume further financial obligations.
That then is the position of the provincial governments as of November 6. They say to the federal government that this situation should be considered a national emergency and that the provincial governments should not be required to assume further financial obligations. The government's offer, of course, was predicated on the provinces accepting additional financial obligations to the extent of paying 50 per cent of the cost.
This is the very type of thing that I suspected would be in this correspondence. It was for these reasons that I said to the Minister of Agriculture that in my opinion the correspondence would show that the provinces had asked the government for something more, that the provinces were united in making these requests and that in this correspondence there would be evidence damaging to the federal government. I think this is very true. The provinces were united in asking the federal government to assume the responsibility of making these payments. The government refused to do so and has forced the provinces to pay half of the cost. I think the correspondence contains precisely the type of thing that I alluded to in my remarks.

I should like to point out that the reading of this letter has added precisely nothing to what I said on February 5 as reported at page 799 of Hansard. The hon. member for Assiniboia had been making a great point of the fact that the provinces had asked us initially to pay the whole cost of this assistance program. In replying to him, as reported at the bottom of that page on the right-hand side, I said as follows:
The hon. member for Assiniboia brought up the point that the provinces initially asked to have the dominion government pay the whole cost of this type of relief. Naturally the provinces asked the dominion government to do so-
I made no bones about the fact that they asked that. I said they asked that. Therefore, as I say, the reading of this letter does not add a bit to the information of the committee. The quotation continues:
-and they follow this course with respect to practically every expenditure that is going to be made. I suppose it is human nature that that should be the case. However, the actual situation is that the primary responsibility for relief or assistance in a situation of this kind rests with the municipalities and the provinces. They are primarily responsible for the assistance which is necessary in situations of this nature.
I then went on to point out that we as a dominion government, just the same as when disasters of various kinds took place in the

past, had recognized this as something to which the dominion government should contribute. As a result we held these numerous conversations with the provinces and had made to them an offer to pay half the cost of the assistance program. The fact that they asked us to assume the whole cost, as I say, I do not think is a material factor. I stated that that was the case to begin with when this matter was up for discussion, so this reading of the letter adds nothing to the information of the committee.

615. Payments to provinces and in respect of Indian bands under the municipal winter works incentive program during the 1959-60 and 1960-61 fiscal years of amounts not exceeding one half of the cost of labour incurred in the period from the 1st day of December, 1959, to the 30th day of April, 1960, in accordance with terms and conditions approved by the governor in council, $15,000,000.
Is the minister not going to say something?

This item of $15 million is for the municipal incentive program similar to the one which we had during the winter of 1958-59. Perhaps the whole amount shown here will not be used up but the funds are there should they be needed. At the outset I would say that the program has been widely accepted by the municipalities across Canada, so much so that they again have asked us to institute this program for this winter of 1959-60. I should like to say a few words about the background of this program.
When this government assumed office we saw that unemployment was rising and that action would have to be taken by this government in order to alleviate the situation. Some of the measures we took have been described on previous occasions, both inside this house and outside. One of the things we did at once was to call a conference of management, labour and other interested parties in this country specifically to deal with the unemployment problem and to give us their advice on this situation. This conference was called in July of 1958.
I should like to note now, Mr. Chairman, that one of the recommendations of this conference was this municipal incentive program. As a matter of fact, many of the recommendations at this conference were based on the incentive aspect. This we did at the time and it was then followed subsequently by a special conference with the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities where this particular incentive stemming from the July

conference was put forward to the government in respect of the participation of municipalities in order to alleviate the seasonal unemployment problem. From the brief of the federation of Canadian mayors and municipalities which was presented to the Prime Minister in April, 1959 1 should like to quote as follows:
This program is substantially along the lines proposed at the special meeting on winter employment called by the Minister of Labour last July and at which representatives of the federation were in attendance, and which proposals were discussed in principle at the informal federal-municipal conference held last October-
As a result of this program-some 32,000 jobs were created during the period.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: How many?

Thirty two thousand. The quotation continues:
The municipal governments were thereby relieved of a potential further cost of direct unemployment relief and, at the same time, were enabled to carry out certain local public works at less cost to the municipalities than otherwise would have been possible

The municipalities are of the view that the municipal winter works program has justified itself and they commend the dominion government for initiating the program.
This was the way in which the municipalities viewed this program at that time and are still viewing it at the present time. So out of this conference in July of 1958 and specifically out of the special conference between the municipalities and this government this program was inaugurated. I would also point out that this conference in July of 1958 and the discussions at this conference also helped to give birth to the $750 million program that built 280,000 homes in two years.
This problem of the municipalities was no new problem. Prior to that time for many years the municipalities endeavoured to interest the federal government in participation in just such a program. The records show that as far back as 1955 representations were made by the municipalities to the federal government to institute such a program. At that time I might say that no action was taken.
However, I want to quote some figures as to what happened last year under this program. There were nearly 2,000 projects and the figure to December of this year is 1,232; that is as of December 31. Last year the federal government spent $6.5 million. In consideration of that rather modest expenditure from the federal treasury, work projects were put into motion totalling nearly $50 million-the actual cost was $49,501,000. This year the estimate is now in the neighbourhood of some $84 million. The cost to the federal treasury is over $10 million as of now. Last 79951-0-58
Supply-Labour
year we provided a little better than 35,000 jobs. I should explain at this time for the benefit of the members of this committee that for every man employed on site on these projects, employment off site is estimated to have been provided for an additional two persons. Hence the figure of 35,000 in direct employment would be further enlarged by an additional 70,000 off site, that is those engaged in industry and the supplying of materials used on these projects. The program this year is still ahead of last year and the figures to the end of January are already over last year's total.
I do not know what else I can add at this time in respect of this program. However, I want to say that I feel that it has been a worth-while program, even though in some instances criticism has been put forth that the program is not sufficient, that it does not take care of the whole situation.
But I say that this is only one of the programs that this government instituted in order to alleviate the situation, as a result of that conference which was held in July, 1958 and the subsequent conference with the municipalities. This is one of the things which were recommended, and it is one of the things which were asked for. This year we did announce the program sooner by two months in order to give municipalities an opportunity to plan ahead of time, and thereby undertake more projects than they were able to last winter.

Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister a question before he resumes his seat. There is reference in this item in the estimates to payments to provinces and in respect of Indian bands. I wonder if the minister would explain what the Indian bands section is, and what is its relationship paymentwise and projectwise between the Indian authorities and the federal government?

Some requests were made approximately a month ago by Indian bands, particularly in the western part of Canada, that they be allowed to be included in this municipal incentive program. The government felt that this was a worthwhile proposal, and consequently they have now been included.
What happens there is that the Indian band deals directly with the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, in the same way as a municipality deals through the province, and then through the citizenship and immigration branch with the Department of Labour and Department of Finance, who ultimately pass on these projects. The Indian bands are putting up 50 per cent of the cost. At least,

Supply-Lab our
we participate in 50 per cent of the labour costs in the same way as we do with the municipalities. The Department of Citizenship and Immigration look over the projects and approve them and send them on to our department for final approval. The same thing will be done with the final payments for these projects; the Department of Citizenship and Immigration will perform that same function in respect of these same bands.

One other question. Does the minister know what the accounting relationship is within the Department of Citizenship and Immigration with regard to these Indian bands, or are they dealt with under the general vote of the Indian affairs branch? What is the internal relationship there?
As far as I know it is that the bands put up their own money.

Mr. Chairman, at the great risk of offending a good many hon. members in this house who seem to think it is improper for some of us on this side to take part in debates, I intend to say something about this item.
It is perhaps appropriate that the debate on this item should be begun by a member of parliament from the province of Newfoundland which enjoys the unhappy distinction, I regret to say, of having the highest level of unemployment of any province in Canada.
They need a better representative.
What they need is a good government in this country.
Oh, oh.

Not only does the province of Newfoundland have the unhappy distinction of having the highest level of unemployment of any province, but the Atlantic region has the highest level of unemployment of any region in this country; and that was, of course, the region in which a new era was going to be introduced after hon. gentlemen won the election of 1957.
I am afraid that I was unable to share the happiness expressed by the Minister of Labour earlier today when he told us that on January 21 over 774,000 Canadians were applying for jobs at the employment offices throughout this country. I would draw the attention of hon. members to the fact, the regrettable fact, a fact which all of us should regret, and none so much as those gentlemen who were going to cure all of these problems a couple of years ago, that this figure of 774,000 persons seeking work in the minister's

own employment offices, apart altogether from a great many others who think it worthless to go there, is not very much below the average figure of 855,000 for the month of January, 1958 which the minister described as the lowest point in the recent recession. Yet the minister told us the other day on T.V. that the recession was now over and everything was all right in this country.
With over three quarters of a million people looking for work from the Minister of Labour's department-
That is not right.

The minister gave us the figure himself, and if the hon. member wants to quarrel with his minister, let him quarrel with his minister and not interfere with my speech. What words did the Prime Minister put in His Excellency's mouth about this?
What are your ideas?

Supply-Labour
Minister believed to be the facts at that time. That is how much discernment he showed. Then we find the minister himself speaking in Montreal on December 10 of that year. Here is what the minister said:
There is hardly an economist or a student of the situation who does not feel that the unemployment situation is merely temporary and that given a brief breathing pause the natural buoyancy of the economy will assert itself.
That was the minister speaking in December, six months after he had come into office. Then, that blinding revelation came to the Prime Minister when he found a dusty book in a drawer. What he could not see with his own eyes, and what the minister could not see with his eyes, what this government which had been in office for seven months had not perceived at all, they blamed Walter Harris for not having told them about nine months earlier. Of course that was the great dramatic performance we witnessed here on January 20, 1958.
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am inclined to think that the hon. member is straying away from the subject under discussion. I feel that the item under consideration does not lead to a general discussion about unemployment.
Oh.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think that if the remarks of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate had been only introductory they might have been in order but I feel that the item is concerned only with the question of financial aid to the municipalities in respect of winter unemployment. Since the rule in committee is to be strictly relevant I think that to initiate a general debate on unemployment on this item would be entirely out of order.

The minister himself in opening the discussion on this item dealt not only with this particular winter works program but with the problem of unemployment in this country as he sees it. Surely we are entitled to say that we do not see the problem in the same way and that this item for winter works is not adequate to meet the problem as we see it. Surely we are entitled to build up the case and condemn the government for directing inadequate attention to this vital national problem.

On the point of order which has been raised, item 615 under discussion is an estimate of $15 million covering the federal government's winter works program in conjunction with the municipalities. I suggest it is impossible to discuss this item in a vacuum. You cannot discuss a $15 million winter works program except in the context [Mr. Pickersgill.l
of the need for a winter works program. I think that ranging far afield, talking of ten years ago, perhaps, and going back into the detailed record of previous administrations would be beyond the scope of this item, but I do feel that the unemployment figures which throw light on the unemployment situation in Canada at this time, and the government's program to deal with the current situation, are very much in order. Anything pertaining to unemployment in Canada at the present time and the government's policy, adequate or inadequate, is very much in order.

In answer to what has been said about my opening remarks in respect of this item I wish to point out, and Hansard will show, that I have been very scrupulous to keep within this particular item and only those things pertaining to the work undertaken under this plan were dealt with by me. I did not range over any other field of employment or unemployment in this country. I dealt only with matters coming strictly within the scope of this item.
Mr. Chairman, may I remind you that the minister did discuss housing at quite considerable length giving a good many statistics.
No, I did not, Mr. Chairman.

I have taken down the
figures he used. The minister claimed that $750 million had been spent by this government to build 280,000 houses. He also discussed the conference with management and labour held in July of 1958. It seems to me that the minister was ranging very widely over the field. The idea that all we can discuss are the projects that the government chooses to bring before us and not discuss the question of whether or not this is an adequate way to meet this problem would, it seems to me, simply deny us any right whatsoever to discuss the most urgent and immediate problem confronting at least three quarters of a million of our fellow citizens.

Mr. Chairman, in reply to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate may I say that the only reason I mentioned the unemployment conference was to point out where the incentive for this program stemmed from. That is where it stemmed from and there followed consultation with the municipalities at a later date. That was the reason for the reference.
If the minister dealt with these subjects I feel we should have the right to discuss them.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I did not rule that hon. members could not discuss unemployment.

What I said was that the item under discussion did not lead to a general debate on unemployment. I am inclined to agree with the remarks of the hon. member for Assini-boia that as long as we discuss unemployment with regard to this item I think it would be in order. I believe the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate will agree that he was ranging much further afield than I have just indicated. I would ask him to co-operate with the Chair in trying to discuss unemployment with regard to this item, or this item with regard to unemployment.

Mr. Chairman, I will endeavour to discuss within the limits the Chair has indicated my reasons for feeling that this is _ a totally inadequate way to deal with this problem. If our freedom of speech is to be abridged by the dictate of the government-
Order. Withdraw.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member may wish to correct that statement which I think is a reflection on the Chair.

I intended no reflection on the Chair. I apologize to the Chair if the Chair considered there was any reflection. I was seeking to reflect on hon. gentlemen opposite, the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Finance, who used to lecture us hour after hour on the rights of parliament and freedom of speech and who boasted on coming in to power about securing the rights of parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Order.
I do not need any lectures from the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I remind the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that the Chair raised the point of order and nobody else.

Mr. Chairman, to return to the question of unemployment, I shall deal with what the minister also told us in the television program in which he was giving us the background for the situation which makes him feel that this program that is now before us is adequate to deal with it. He said:
You will recall that approximately 18 months ago-
Eighteen months ago was August 4, 1958, if I do my arithmetic correctly. We had been told at other times, of course, that the recession was inherited from us, but this was a year after we were out of office. In any event, this is what the minister said:
You will recall that approximately 18 months ago, when recession was setting in, your government announced bold and progressive policies to combat that recession and to provide jobs for Canadians.
Supply-Labour
What did happen, not precisely on August 4 but on August 16 here in this chamber? I will remind you what happened. It was a Saturday afternoon and the minister will not forget it. I appealed to the minister to hold up one item of his estimates so that we could have the winter work program brought before us. I made an appeal to the minister three times. My friend the hon. member for Laurier then appealed to the then leader of the house who is now the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
During the course of that afternoon the Prime Minister came into the house. The hon. member for Laurier appealed to the Prime Minister to hold up this item and bring on the government's winter work program so that parliament, the elected representatives of the people, would know what the government was going to do about this problem at the very time the minister now tells us the recession was setting in, and we were refused. It was not until late in September on the eve of his world tour that the Prime Minister went to Regina to attend-if my memory serves me correctly-a provincial Tory convention and there announced the winter work program that parliament was not considered fit to hear. That was what was done on that occasion. At least this time an item is brought before us but again we are denied any information at all.
Nonsense.

The hon. gentleman can read Hansard for August 16 for himself.
The minister then went on to attempt to show that this seasonal unemployment was something that was characteristic of Canada, that there was nothing new about it. While I should like to deal with that part of his speech I agree that it would perhaps not be strictly relevant to this debate for me to do so. I did notice that in the minister's efforts to minimize the situation we are now faced with and to make it appear that it is just the same sort of thing that existed ever since the war he gave a number of figures which, from my point of view did not prove that at all.
What I do think is very relevant to the situation now and very serious as well is that according to the base the minister was using-and that is the dominion bureau of statistics base-the unemployment in this country was 10 per cent of the labour force in March of 1958. Last year it was 8.6 per cent and according to the minister's own figures it was 5.9 per cent in December of last year.
I draw to your attention, sir, the fact that 5.9 per cent on the dominion bureau of statistics base, which we do not consider to

Supply-Labour
be an adequate measure, was the figure applicable in December of last year and in March of 1957. In March of 1957, when hon. members opposite are fond of saying a depression was taking place, the figure was 5.9 per cent and in December of 1959 when the minister was telling the people of Canada the recession was over it was the same figure. That figure is very much higher today and unhappily it is still going up.
If the recession is over, and I am not questioning that in the ordinary sense of the term it is, it has left a residue of a high level of unemployment which is not going to be dealt with adequately by a puny measure of this sort.
A puny measure of this sort?

Yes, a puny measure of this sort. When three quarters of a million of our fellow citizens are applying at the minister's offices for jobs, a puny measure of this sort is not going to deal adequately with the problem.
Tell that to the people of Brome-Missisquoi.

The hon. gentleman can go down along the coasts to the places from which I get letters every day from people with families asking for jobs, people who have no unemployment insurance, people who have been forced on relief, and tell them there is no unemployment problem in this country. We who come from these areas know that there is this condition, and we do not think it should be a matter of jest.
That is not what Joey said in New York.

I say again that with three quarters of a million of our fellow citizens applying for jobs in the minister's own offices, this is not an adequate measure.
I say it is not an adequate measure for another reason. I know that one of my colleagues is going to ask the minister, before this item passes, to put on the record the details of where these projects are. I know, too, if it is anything like the pattern of the last two years we will find, as we do tend to find with all these 50-50 sharing programs, that they are strictly programs that illustrate the truth of the statement that to him that hath shall be given. These municipalities that are comparatively wealthy, with a comparatively large tax base, are able to take advantage of this offer and get on with needed and useful works. No one is sorry to see that happen. However, in those areas where unemployment is greatest the capacity of the municipalities to embark on these works, 
because of their own narrow tax base, is the least. A 50-50 basis is not a satisfactory basis at all for a program of this sort.
It does seem to me it should not be beyond the ingenuity of this government and this house to find a formula which would, as between provinces and even perhaps areas within provinces, relate the principles of division somewhat to the level of unemployment. Then in those areas of heavy unemployment, for example in Cape Breton, in Newfoundland and in the county of Pictou where conditions are very serious at the present time, and indeed all through the Atlantic region and in the eastern part of Quebec where the level of unemployment is a great deal higher than it is in the rest of the country and where the local capacity to deal with it is a great deal lower, there would be a better formula for this kind of program. If there were there is no question but that many of these municipalities, if they only had to pay 25 per cent instead of 50 per cent of the cost, might be able to carry on these programs. However, they cannot, and the program is really ineffective in precisely those areas where it is most important that it should be effective.
It does not seem to me, that this is the right way to deal with this problem. This is one element, I grant the minister that it is one element. However, my hon. friend from Trinity made a very moving speech in this house a year ago, a very thoughtful speech, about the changing character of our labour force. I think you will find this is directly related to the problem here. The fact is that more and more skills are required in order to get employment in this modern world. It does seem to me that the government and the minister received that speech very well, but with words. I do wish those words were being followed by deeds.
They are.

All over this country and particularly in the eastern part, the need for such training of adult workers in order to enable them to take advantage of the opportunities for employment is very pressing indeed. A lot of this human waste of unemployment could be remedied. There are still a good many areas in which there is a scarcity of labour. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration told us the other day she is still lending money for assisted passages for people coming to Canada to take jobs. I have here an advertisement which gives a whole list of occupations in Canada for which people in the United Kingdom can get a loan to come to Canada to take work. They are all skills. I wish the minister would give

us a list, while this debate is on, of those skills in which there are job opportunities in this country at the present time.
I wish more advertising would be done in that connection and an effort made to train the people in this country who are unemployed, and not just seasonally unemployed unhappily, to take advantage of the opportunities offered in certain fields. Unless these people do get some skills a good many of them will never be employed again, except on very rare occasions. It seems to me if we are going to take this problem seriously, tackle it seriously, it is in that direction and not just in palliatives, however desirable they may be, that the solution will be found.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes, certainly.

The hon. member referred to the training of the unemployed in Canada. Would he perhaps use his influence with the premier of Newfoundland to carry out a training scheme on Bell island that has been offered by the Minister of Labour?
I would be glad to use my influence with anybody anywhere in this country if my influence would extend anywhere to see that any of the unemployed in this country who need training got training.
There are 600 Bell islanders waiting for that.

Before I proceed to discuss the item under consideration, may I say that I tried to copy down some figures which the minister related to the committee during his opening remarks. If I may make a brief reference to them perhaps the minister would indicate whether or not I have copied them down correctly. I understood the minister to say that the winter works program or the municipal winter works program for this current winter season has, at the present time, $10 million committed by the federal government, with projects valued at $84 million under consideration, about to start or under construction. I wonder whether the minister could indicate whether or not those figures are correct?
There is one phase of this problem in which I have a special interest and that is the relationship of this winter works program to Indian bands and projects on Indian reserves. However, I feel it is rather unfortunate that the minister did not have available a detailed explanation of the relationship between the Indian bands which will be interested in participating in this program and the Indian affairs branch of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. The minister did say
Supply

Labour
the bands themselves would be required, so far as he knows, to supply the money for their part of the project. If this is so, it is an extremely unwise and unfair policy to follow.
It may be beneficial to those few Indian bands who because of geographic or other conditions have been able to accumulate some money in their band funds and thus are able to participate financially in this type of project but it is extremely unfair and discriminatory in the case of those Indian bands which may not have any money in their band fund accounts or only a few dollars. I know that there are quite a few bands throughout the country that have no band fund account because of the economy of the reserve and things of that nature. I would appreciate it very much if the minister would take up the matter with the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration so that he will be able to give us a clearer understanding of this matter because if the minister is correct in saying that the band itself from its own band fund account must find the money for the project then it is an extremely unfair, unwise and discriminatory action to take against bands that do not have any money in their band fund accounts.

Mr. Chairman, the action was not instituted by the government. The Indian bands themselves requested that they be allowed to participate under this plan since they were prepared to put up their money.

That is precisely what I am getting at. What you are doing is confining participation in this project to those bands that have sufficient money in their band fund accounts to be able to afford to do this.
It was their proposition.
You are a party to it.
We acquiesced in it.

Why do you not make it uniformly applicable to all Indian bands in the country instead of confining it to those few bands that may have enough money to participate in some sort of program? It is extremely unfair, unwise and discriminatory in the case of those bands which unfortunately, for one reason or another, have no money in their band fund accounts. Even though the minister has said that the government did not initiate this, I think he would be well advised to consult his colleague the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and attempt to work out a policy whereby the Indian affairs branch of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration will provide the money for those bands which do not have the money in their band fund accounts. That

Supply-Labour
is what I am saying is unfair, and I would certainly appreciate it if the minister would undertake to press for the inclusion of these other Indian bands in this type of program even though their share may have to be paid out of the funds of the Indian affairs branch.
Apart from the application to Indian bands, which is a specific phase of the matter, in presenting this program the minister lauded it and the government's initiation of it. He also made reference to a few conferences that were held and the program that arose out of them. But it is very unfortunate that this municipal works program, no matter how he attempts to varnish it, is being used to cover up the failure of the government to meet its commitments at election time.
No matter how much the minister tries to talk about the number of people who will be employed under the program and the number of people who will be employed under the housing program, in no way can that do away with the damage that was done to the nation by the Tory party through its irrational and phony promises about full employment. They went all over the country telling the people how they were going to bring about full employment-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: And did nothing about it, absolutely nothing.

-but as soon as they got into office they decided that the promises that they made to the nation were not the ones that should be kept, that they should only keep promises made to parliament, as the Minister of National Revenue later said. On one occasion the Prime Minister, almost with tears in his voice, said, "Not one person will sufEer from unemployment". But what are we getting? A program of this nature, this substitute for the carrying out of the agreement they made with the Canadian people on March 31, 1958, this substitute for the contract they entered into to provide full employment so that not one person would sufEer. This is the way their contract has been carried out even though the general public carried out their part of the bargain and elected them to office.
Deficit or no deficit.

That is a minor detail. The hon. gentleman who handles the purse strings and most other strings in the cabinet is in his seat tonight and appears to nod acceptance of my statement, I see. This type of program was probably born one day when the Prime Minister rose from his bed and got the bright idea of sending a telegram to the various provinces indicating that they were willing to put up a certain amount

of money. This has become a year-to-year policy because of this idea the Prime Minister had and because the government has failed or has been unable to carry out any planned, co-ordinated program to deal with unemployment. This represents nothing more than another exemplification of the haphazard, step-by-step, year-by-year efforts that the government is making in a faltering way to attempt to deal with a problem that it has not got the foggiest idea how to cope with.
It is too bad you are not dealing with it.

Normal, seasonal, recurring unemployment is what it is now. It is not a national problem as it was during the election year. If it is a normal, recurring, seasonal unemployment situation, that is, during spring, summer, fall and winter; if it is that sort of thing then there is all the more reason that the government should draft legislation to provide a planned, coordinated long range program to deal with it on a seasonal basis instead of bringing forward a supplementary estimate once a year and saying that they need a few more million dollars because they did not quite cope with the problem last year and they find they are going to have to deal with it again.
Not only that, but the program is far too restrictive in its application. The initial plan that was given to the nation when the Prime Minister sent his telegram was that 50 per cent of the responsibility was going to be carried by the federal government. That was the impression that the government tried to leave with the nation. This big hearted, generous Minister of Finance, who has had a relapse since those days, was going to pay 50 per cent of the cost of such municipal projects. But what do we find now? We find that the amount is closer to 10 to 12 per cent than 50 per cent because of the restrictions in the program itself. In the meantime, as my friend from Bonavista-Twillingate pointed out-
Your friend?
If I can call the Conservatives in this house my friends they will not object to my calling the Liberals my friends.
We are a little fussy.

My friend says that he is a little fussy. He should consider those he has for friends who sit on the front benches. Some people should be a little upset to have to call people like that their friends. You may be fussy as to your friends. I will withdraw what I said, Mr. Chairman, as I know

I should under the rules. I will withdraw every reference I have made in the house to any Conservative member being a friend of mine. I will use the proper parliamentary designation and call them hon. members, and even that is stretching it.
1 am sure there are three quarters of a million people in this country knocking on the door of the Minister of Labour who do not care whether the people in this house are friends or not or what we call each other. They are concerned about getting employment and they are not going to be put off with any two-bit, peanut type program that the minister took from a brainwave that the Prime Minister had which resulted in his sending out a telegram and saying that this was going to be it forever and ever, amen. They are not going to be satisfied with that sort of thing and they are not going to be satisfied with the two major parties, the official opposition and the government, having an annual game of debating which set of statistics applies to these people.
The minister would have done well to take the advice I gave him a couple of years ago when I said he should stand in the breadlines with some of these people and find out how they feel. Then he would realize that this is not a normal recurring seasonal unemployment problem. He would realize that these three quarters of a million people are not just figures in a set of books but that they represent people, families including children, that have the same needs and desires as has the minister and everybody in this house. That is what we should be concerned with rather than concerning ourselves with the actual statistics and the relationship that the winter works program might have to that over-all unemployment picture which exists in this country today, which existed last year and the year before that, and which existed whenever this government or its predecessor were in office because neither one of them know how to cope with the economic problems that are confronting the nation and are getting worse every day.
We have had references to an increase in production and to an expansion in the economy of the nation. It is said that 1960 is going to be a boom year. It is said that we are not going to overcome the recession but that we have overcome it already. With three quarters of a million people knocking on the minister's back door looking for some sort of employment, it is said that we have overcome the recession. If these things are true, and there is every indication that they are true in so far as projecting this current year is concerned, that things started to
Supply-Labour
pick up in the last quarter of the last year, that there is an increase in the economy, an increase in the productivity figures or an increase in the national production of the country, it is also shown that along with this increase in productivity and increase in economic expansion there has not been the concomitant or relative increase in the employment picture of the nation, that the number of employed have not kept up with the increase in the productivity itself and that it far outstrips this increase. Although we may have greater productivity, may have increased production, may have a greater volume of goods being produced in the nation, we have not been able to get that increase reflected in an increase in the number of people employed in the nation at productive work for if we had we would not have three quarters of a million people now unemployed and seeking work in this nation.
I am sure one can be harsh with this government for having made an election pledge and having promptly forgotten it. We could lay all the blame on the government. This is playing a little bit of politics, I expect. We could-and probably this will happen in this debate later on-make fairly heated arguments about this sort of thing. Even though there is a tremendous responsibility on and a tremendous fault resting with the government because it has not the courage to plan accordingly to meet these recurring problems and the new problems which will arise because of the economic change in the country, because of the growth of industry or from expansion or from consolidation, I think we also must look at the economy itself and wonder what we can do to ensure that these ups and downs, booms and busts, "recurring seasonal unemployments" or whatever phrase the Prime Minister used to make reference to three quarters of a million people being out of work, do not occur. We must look at economic conditions and say, how can we cope with this particular sort of thing?
I know that there are in the government services economists who are wondering along these very same lines, who are wondering about how we can arrange to conduct our business affairs in this nation so that we shall be able to compete with other nations on the trade question. I appreciate that this is going a bit beyond the scope of the winter works program but I think it is connected because if we had a decently run economy I do not think we would be in the difficulty we are now in and we would not have this thing before us. But these economists are groping around, silently mostly, because no one on the government benches has asked them to sit down and attempt to deal with this

Supply-Labour
particular question and to come up with some long range recommendations as to what the government can do to overcome it on a planned long term basis, not to overcome it from day to day or from year to year as the minister is asking us to do at the present time.
Carried.
Ten o'clock.
My friend over there may want to call it ten o'clock but from where we sit there are still two or three minutes to go.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

The hon. member for
Bonavista-Twillingate made some reference to this government's having adopted a philosophy that it is all right to have a great number of people unemployed either at certain times during the year or throughout the year itself. I suggest that unfortunately this philosophy, if this present Tory government has it, is one which they inherited from their predecessors the Liberals when they were in office because they had precisely the same sort of idea, that it is all right to have employment once in a while, that it is necessary, that it is an integral part of our economy and that there is no sense in worrying too much about it; that we will just give out a few unemployment cheques once in a while as a palliative, as the hon. member called it, as some sort of dole or relief to the poor unemployed person who happens to be unemployed but we will not tackle the over-all basic question of dealing with unemployment itself.
This is where the Liberals failed when they were in office and this is where the present Tory government is failing, because it is unable or unwilling to cope with this broad over-all question. I wish the Minister of
Labour himself and his colleague in the Department of Trade and Commerce or the Department of Finance, depending on who the principal powerful person is in the cabinet at any one particular time, would issue some definite instructions to the economists in the government service for study and investigation in order to attempt to come up with some sort of program that will deal with this question effectively and adequately on a long range planned basis instead of the very ineffective method that is being used or is shown as being used not only in this particular vote but in many others that come before the house from time to time.
I wonder, Mr. Chairman, if I might at this stage call it ten o'clock.
Resolutions adopted in committee of supply this day reported and concurred in.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I take it that tomorrow and Thursday we will deal with the debate on foreign affairs, as agreed. I wonder whether the minister will tell us what we shall be doing on Friday.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Wednesday and Thursday, as mentioned, the debate on foreign affairs as the house agreed the other day; on Friday a continuation of consideration of the supplementary estimates. If those are completed, we shall take the government business that is on the order paper and I will announce the specific items on Thursday.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Might I go a step further and ask the leader of the house what we may expect on Monday.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I think perhaps I will announce that on Thursday.
At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing orders.
